title: Two pushes make a steady level: sugar, breath, pulse and pupils

summary.text: A small bottle of cola holds about six teaspoons of sugar. All the blood in a grown-up holds only about one teaspoon. Yet after the cola, the sugar in the blood hardly moves. The body does it with two opposite pushes. One hormone pulls sugar out of the blood, and another puts it back. You build a bottle that keeps its own water level, race your pulse and breathing back to rest, and watch your pupils correct themselves faster than you can decide anything. A steady level turns out to be a lot of work.
summary.art: A boy on a tightrope-style wire in a living room, leaning left, with a small bottle of cola on a table below and a single teaspoon of sugar on a saucer beside it.

intro.hook: Stand on one leg for 20 seconds and look at your foot. It seems still, but it is not. Your ankle is shaking a little, left, right, left. Why does a thing that looks still need so much movement?
intro.text: Your body keeps many things steady. You already know about warmth and water. Now look at sugar, breath, pulse and the black dots in your eyes. All of them stay near a good level, and all of them do it the same way. Something pushes up, and something else pushes down. Where the two pushes meet, the level stays. In this unit you find those two pushes in a plastic bottle, in your ankle, in your blood and in your eyes.
intro.art: A child standing on one leg in a kitchen, with thin arrows drawn on the ankle pointing left and right, and a faint wobbly outline of the foot around it.

outcomes: I can explain that a steady level is made by two opposite pushes working at once, and not by nothing happening.
I can use a bottle with a hole to show that the bigger a change is, the stronger the push back.
I can describe how insulin and glucagon keep the sugar in my blood steady.
I can explain why we feel the urge to breathe, and measure how my pulse and breathing come back to rest.
I can show with a pupil test that a body loop can correct itself in about a second, without me deciding.
I can explain why a loop with a delay can swing past the right level, using a game of warmer and colder.
I can say what goes wrong when a loop breaks, as in diabetes, and who found out how to help.

terms.meaning: The body keeping things such as warmth, water and sugar near a good level, even when the outside changes.
terms.example: Your body stays near 37 degrees on a hot day and a cold day.
terms.art: A child in a hot scene and a cold scene, with the same small 37 badge on the chest in both.

terms.meaning: The level the body is trying to hold. Control systems compare the real level with the set point.
terms.example: Your body's set point for warmth is near 37 degrees.
terms.art: A dial with a green zone in the middle and a small pointer sitting in it.

terms.meaning: A loop in which a change causes a push in the opposite direction. The bigger the change, the bigger the push back.
terms.example: A deeper bottle leaks faster, so the water level stops rising.
terms.art: Two arrows in a circle: an up arrow labelled 'level rises' and a down arrow labelled 'push back'.

terms.meaning: A level that stays the same because the flow in and the flow out are equal, while both keep going.
terms.example: The water level in a bottle with a hole and a trickle stays steady while water flows through.
terms.art: A bottle with a trickle entering the top and a thin jet leaving a hole near the base, level line marked.

terms.meaning: Two controls that push in opposite directions, so the body can correct a change either way.
terms.example: Insulin lowers blood sugar, and glucagon raises it.
terms.art: A see-saw with a small arrow pushing down on one end and another arrow pushing up on the other end.

terms.meaning: The simple sugar that travels in your blood and feeds your cells. Your body makes it from the food you eat.
terms.example: Rice, rotis and fruit are all turned into glucose.
terms.art: A small bowl of rice and a roti with dotted arrows leading to a red blood vessel carrying tiny sugar cubes.

terms.meaning: A hormone that tells cells to take glucose out of the blood. It lowers the sugar level in the blood.
terms.example: After a sweet meal, insulin rises and the blood sugar comes back down.
terms.art: A key shaped like a tiny gate opener approaching a cell with a glucose door.

terms.meaning: A hormone that tells the liver to put stored sugar back into the blood. It raises the sugar level.
terms.example: Between meals, glucagon stops your blood sugar from falling too low.
terms.art: A liver with a small tap opening and tiny sugar cubes flowing into a blood vessel.

terms.meaning: A gland behind the stomach that makes insulin, glucagon and digestive juices.
terms.example: The pancreas is about the size of a banana in a grown-up.
terms.art: An outline of a body with the stomach and a long, flat, leaf-shaped pancreas behind it.

terms.meaning: A chemical message made in one part of the body and carried in the blood to another part.
terms.example: Insulin is a hormone that goes from the pancreas to cells all over the body.
terms.art: A tiny envelope sailing in a blood vessel from a gland to a cell.

terms.meaning: A condition in which the body cannot keep blood sugar steady, because insulin is missing or does not work well.
terms.example: A person with type 1 diabetes takes insulin from outside, as injections or from a pump.
terms.art: A child checking a small sensor on the arm while a grown-up looks at a phone showing a gentle line graph.

terms.meaning: The beat you can feel in an artery each time your heart pushes blood out.
terms.example: Press two fingers on your wrist and count the beats in 15 seconds.
terms.art: Two fingers resting on the inside of a wrist with small circles spreading out at each beat.

terms.meaning: A gas your cells make when they use food for energy. You breathe it out. It is the main signal that tells you to breathe.
terms.example: When you run, your cells make more carbon dioxide, and you breathe faster.
terms.art: Tiny grey molecules leaving a cell, entering the blood and leaving the nose in a breath.

terms.meaning: The black opening in the middle of the eye that lets light in. It gets smaller in bright light and bigger in dim light.
terms.example: In a dark room, your pupils open wide to catch more light.
terms.art: A close drawing of an eye with a large black pupil in dim light and a small one in bright light, side by side.

terms.meaning: A fast automatic response that happens without you deciding.
terms.example: Your pupils shrink when a bright light comes on.
terms.art: An eye, a small arrow to the brain stem and a small arrow back to the eye muscle.

terms.meaning: When a correction goes past the right level, because the effect arrives late.
terms.example: A hot-and-cold shower tap swings too hot, then too cold, if the water takes time to arrive.
terms.art: A line graph with a wobble: the line goes above the target, below it, then settles.

explanations.concept: A steady level is two flows that match
explanations.definition: A level stays steady when what comes in equals what goes out. Scientists call this a dynamic balance.
explanations.description: A bottle with a small hole and a slow trickle of water going in fills up to a certain level and stops. The water has not stopped moving. Water pours in at the top and leaks out of the hole at the same speed. If more comes in than goes out, the level rises. If more goes out than comes in, the level falls. It stays flat only when the two are equal. Your body's levels work the same way. Your blood has sugar going in from food and from the liver, and sugar going out into cells. The level is flat because both flows are going all the time.
examples: A bucket under a dripping tap with a hole in the bucket.
A river that keeps the same shape while its water changes every second.
The sugar in your blood, which stays near one level while meals come and go.
explanations.art: A bottle with a trickle entering at the top and a jet leaving a hole near the bottom, with arrows of equal length for 'in' and 'out' and a dotted level line.

explanations.concept: Negative feedback: the bigger the change, the bigger the push back
explanations.definition: Negative feedback is a loop in which a change causes a push in the opposite direction, and a bigger change causes a bigger push.
explanations.description: Why does the water level in the bottle stop at one height and not another? Deeper water pushes harder on the hole, so it leaks out faster. As the level rises, the leak grows, until the leak matches the trickle. The level itself works as the sensor. A body does the same with a hormone or a nerve. When blood sugar rises, the pancreas sends out more insulin. The higher the sugar, the more insulin. That pulls the level back down. In L3 you met the body's warmth loop. This is the same idea, with the push back growing in size with the change.
examples: A deeper bottle leaks faster.
More sugar in the blood brings out more insulin.
A pressure cooker lifts its whistle higher when the steam pushes harder, and lets out more steam.
explanations.art: Two bottles side by side: a low level with a thin leak, and a high level with a strong jet, with a bar showing 'bigger change, bigger push back'.

explanations.concept: Why the body uses opposing pairs
explanations.definition: An opposing pair is two controls that push in opposite directions, so a level can be corrected whether it went too high or too low.
explanations.description: One control can only push one way. If insulin were the only control, it could bring sugar down, but nothing could bring it back up if it dropped too low. So the body has a second control, glucagon, that pushes up. Sweating and shivering are another pair, and so are the two muscles at the front and back of your upper arm. When you balance on one leg, muscles on both sides of the ankle pull in turn. Having two opposite controls lets the body correct a mistake in both directions, and also lets it stop at the right place instead of sliding past.
examples: Insulin lowers blood sugar and glucagon raises it.
Sweating cools you and shivering warms you.
The biceps bends your elbow and the triceps straightens it.
explanations.art: A see-saw with a body outline in the middle, insulin pushing down on one side and glucagon pushing up on the other, and a small ball (the sugar level) resting near the middle.

explanations.concept: Blood sugar: who puts it in, who takes it out
explanations.definition: Blood sugar is the glucose carried in your blood. A healthy body keeps it within a narrow range, between meals and after them.
explanations.description: When you eat rice, roti, fruit or a laddu, your gut turns the starch and sugar into glucose, and it enters your blood. Your cells need glucose for energy. Your brain alone uses about a fifth of all the energy your body makes, mostly from glucose. After a meal, special cells in the pancreas, called beta cells, release insulin. Insulin tells muscle, fat and liver cells to take glucose in, and the liver to store it as a starchy store called glycogen. Hours after a meal, when the blood sugar starts to fall, alpha cells in the pancreas release glucagon. It tells the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose. In a grown-up, all the blood holds only about 4 to 5 grams of glucose, about one teaspoon. A child has less blood and so less. Everything that goes in and out of that small amount is steered by the two hormones.
examples: After a sweet meal, insulin rises and the sugar level comes back down.
After a long gap between meals, glucagon rises and the level does not fall.
During a long walk, muscles use up glucose and the liver keeps topping it up.
explanations.art: A cutaway body: food entering the gut, glucose in the blood as tiny cubes, the pancreas sending a down-arrow (insulin) and an up-arrow (glucagon) to the liver and cells.

explanations.definition: Diabetes is a condition in which the body cannot keep blood sugar steady, because insulin is missing or does not work well.
explanations.description: In type 1 diabetes, the body's own defence system destroys the beta cells, so the pancreas makes almost no insulin. Without insulin, glucose piles up in the blood and cells go short of it. This begins mostly in childhood or youth. Before 1922 it was often fatal within a year or two. Today people with type 1 diabetes give themselves insulin by injection or from a pump, and check their sugar with sensors, so they do the second push themselves. In type 2 diabetes, insulin is made but the cells respond less well to it, and later the pancreas can tire. It is much more common and is linked to genes, body weight, food and exercise. About 101 million people in India were found to have diabetes in a large 2023 study. Both types can be managed with good care. A doctor should always guide treatment. Rosalyn Yalow, an American scientist, helped show with Solomon Berson in the 1950s that many adults with diabetes have insulin in their blood that is not working well. Dorothy Hodgkin worked out the shape of the insulin molecule in 1969.
examples: A child with type 1 diabetes injects insulin before meals and checks sugar with a sensor.
A grown-up with type 2 diabetes may take tablets, walk daily and change their food.
A glucose meter or a sensor is a sensor in a loop that a person completes with insulin.
explanations.art: A girl wearing a small round sensor on her upper arm, checking a phone with a gentle line graph, with a pen of insulin on the table beside a plate of idli.

explanations.concept: What makes you want to breathe
explanations.definition: Your urge to breathe is driven mostly by the amount of carbon dioxide in your blood, and only partly by how little oxygen there is.
explanations.description: Your cells use oxygen and make carbon dioxide all the time. When carbon dioxide builds up in your blood, it makes the blood a little more acidic. Sensors in your brainstem, the part of the brain just above the spinal cord, notice this and speed up your breathing, and breathing out clears the carbon dioxide away. That is why the urge to breathe after holding your breath comes in waves and gets strong before your oxygen is low. Smaller sensors in your neck arteries react to very low oxygen, for example at high altitude. This is also why you should never take big breaths before holding your breath in water. Taking big breaths blows off carbon dioxide, so the urge to breathe comes late, and a person can faint under water without a warning.
examples: After running, you breathe fast because your cells made extra carbon dioxide.
When you hold your breath, the urge to breathe grows in waves before you feel faint.
While you sleep, your brainstem keeps your breathing going without your attention.
explanations.art: A cell sending grey carbon dioxide molecules into a blood vessel, a small sensor in the brainstem, and a nose breathing out the extra carbon dioxide.

explanations.concept: Pulse and breathing: speeding up and slowing back down
explanations.definition: When you exercise, your pulse and breathing speed up and then fall back to rest in a curve: fast at first, then slower.
explanations.description: When your muscles work harder, they use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide. Your heart beats faster and your breathing deepens to bring oxygen and clear carbon dioxide. When you stop, the demand drops, and your pulse falls quickly in the first minute, then more slowly, until it reaches rest. People who are fitter often have a lower pulse at rest and a pulse that falls faster after exercise. At rest, most children of 6 to 10 have a pulse between about 70 and 110 beats a minute and breathe about 16 to 25 times a minute. Your numbers may differ, and they are not a score. Rest levels also change with the time of day, being nervous or excited, and being ill.
examples: Your pulse is highest right after you stop running and falls fast in the first minute.
You still breathe hard for a minute after a race because your body is clearing carbon dioxide.
A fitter person's pulse comes back to rest sooner.
explanations.art: A line graph of pulse against time: low at rest, a sharp rise during exercise, a steep fall in the first minute and a slow fall back to rest.

explanations.concept: Pupils: a fast loop the brain runs without you
explanations.definition: The pupil light reflex is the automatic change in pupil size when the light changes: smaller in bright light and bigger in dim light.
explanations.description: Light reaches the back of your eye and a signal goes to the brainstem, which sends a message back to two sets of tiny muscles in the coloured part of your eye, the iris. One set, shaped like a ring, makes the pupil smaller. The other set, spread out like the spokes of a wheel, makes it bigger. This is another opposing pair. The whole loop takes less than a second, and you do not have to decide anything. Pupils range from about 2 millimetres in bright light to 8 millimetres in the dark. A pupil can also change when you are surprised, interested or frightened. Doctors shine a small light in the eyes of an injured person to check that this reflex works, because it shows that the brainstem is working.
examples: Walking from a bright street into a dark shop, your vision slowly improves as your pupils open.
A cat's pupils shrink to thin slits in bright sun.
Your pupils widen when you see something that interests you.
explanations.art: Two close-up eyes: a bright-light eye with a tiny pupil, ring muscles drawn around it, and a dark eye with a wide pupil and spoke-like muscles drawn outward.

explanations.concept: Delay and overshoot: why corrections swing
explanations.definition: Overshoot happens when a correction arrives late, so the level goes past the target before it settles.
explanations.description: Think of a shower where the hot water takes 10 seconds to reach you. The water is cold, so you turn the tap to hot. Nothing changes yet, so you turn it more. Then the hot water arrives, far too hot, so you turn it back too far. Now it is too cold again. You swing hot and cold until you learn to turn slowly and wait. Any loop with a delay can do this. The body reduces the problem by predicting. When you smell food, your pancreas can release a small first burst of insulin before the sugar arrives. Even so, loops sometimes overshoot, and this is why a person with diabetes can feel shaky when a dose of insulin turns out to be too large.
examples: A shower tap swings hot and cold when the water is slow to arrive.
A blood sugar that falls too low when too much insulin is given.
A cyclist who swerves left and right when learning to steer.
explanations.art: A graph of temperature against time, wobbling above and below a target line and slowly settling, beside a hand on a shower tap.

explanations.concept: Set points can move: fever, sleep and the clock
explanations.description: Many books say the body has one fixed set point. But your set points move. Your body is a little cooler in the early morning and warmer in the late afternoon. During a fever, chemicals released when the body fights an infection tell the brain to raise the warmth set point. That is why a person with a fever shivers while their body is already warmer than usual, because the body is still below its new target. When the fever breaks, the set point goes back and the person sweats. Some scientists say we should describe this as allostasis, which means keeping steady by changing, with targets that are shifted to suit the day. Whether a fever helps or hurts is still argued. Doctors advise seeing a doctor for a baby with a fever, a very high fever, or a fever that lasts.
examples: A fever raises the warmth set point.
Resting pulse and warmth are lower at night than in the afternoon.
Blood pressure rises while you run and falls when you rest.
explanations.art: A day clock with a wavy line of body warmth rising from morning to late afternoon, and a second line showing a fever pushing the set point higher.

perspectives.explanation: The body has fixed set points, such as 37 degrees, and each loop works to bring the level back to its set point.
The body changes its set points to match what is coming, such as the day, a meal, a run or an illness. Steady means steady enough for what is needed.

explanations.concept: When a loop pushes the same way: positive feedback
explanations.definition: Positive feedback is a loop in which a change causes more of the same change.
explanations.description: Most body loops push back, but a few push forward on purpose and then stop. When you cut your finger, the first platelets that stick at the cut release chemicals that call more platelets, and more still, until a plug seals the hole. Once the cut is sealed, the calling stops. In a nerve cell, a small electrical change opens channels that cause a bigger change, so a nerve signal fires like a spark. A microphone too close to its speaker squeals the same way, because the sound gets louder each time round. Positive feedback is good for sealing a cut or sending a signal quickly. But it has to be switched off by something, or it runs away.
examples: A cut finger: more platelets call more platelets until the cut is sealed.
A microphone and speaker squealing.
A nerve cell firing a signal.
explanations.art: A cut on a finger with tiny platelets snowballing into a plug, and a circle of arrows labelled 'more, more, more' ending at a small 'stop' sign.

explanations.concept: The same two pushes outside the body
explanations.description: A guard cell on a leaf works as a tiny pair: when it swells with water the pore between two guard cells opens to take in carbon dioxide, and when it loses water the pore closes to save water. The plant adjusts this all day. Further out, a star stays the same size for billions of years because gravity pulls inwards and the pressure of hot gas pushes outwards, and the two are equal. In a forest, deer and tigers can keep each other's numbers in range. When there are many deer, tigers have more to eat and their numbers grow, and then the deer become fewer. In the 1920s Alfred Lotka and Vito Volterra wrote maths that showed such rises and falls. Real forests are messier than the maths, and it is still argued how much they truly balance.
examples: A leaf's guard cells opening and closing a pore.
The Sun staying the same size because gravity and pressure are equal.
Deer and tigers keeping each other's numbers in range, with swings.
explanations.art: Three small panels: a leaf pore with two guard cells, a glowing star with arrows pulling in and pushing out, and a forest with deer and a tiger and a looping arrow between them.

agreed.text: A healthy body keeps the sugar in its blood inside a narrow range, between meals and after them.
agreed.evidence: Blood tests taken before and after meals in healthy people show the level rising a little and returning to the same range.

agreed.text: Insulin lowers blood sugar and glucagon raises it. They are made by different cells in the pancreas.
agreed.evidence: Injecting purified insulin lowered the sugar in diabetic animals and people from 1921 and 1922. Glucagon was found in 1923 and later shown to raise blood sugar.

agreed.text: The urge to breathe comes mostly from carbon dioxide building up in the blood, and only partly from low oxygen.
agreed.evidence: In 1905 John Scott Haldane and J. G. Priestley measured that a tiny rise in the carbon dioxide in the air people breathe made them breathe much more.

agreed.text: The pupil light reflex is a quick automatic loop through the brainstem. It does not need any thought.
agreed.evidence: It works in people who are drowsy or under anaesthetic, and doctors use it to check the brainstem.

agreed.text: A loop with a delay can overshoot the target and swing, unless the push is gentle or the body predicts.
agreed.evidence: Engineers see it in thermostats, ships' steering and cruise control. Physiologists see it in studies of shaking hands and blood pressure.

agreed.text: Type 1 diabetes happens when the body's own defences destroy the cells that make insulin.
agreed.evidence: Doctors find these damaged cells and the defence cells that attack them in people with the condition.

challenging.claim: A steady reading means that nothing is happening.
challenging.who: Many people, and many textbook pictures of a flat line.
challenging.for: The number really does not change. A flat line on a chart looks as if nothing is going on.
challenging.against: In the Level Bottle, the level stopped rising while water poured through all the time. In the body, a flat sugar level hides insulin and glucagon working. A steady level can be a lot of activity.

challenging.claim: The body has one fixed set point for each thing, such as 37 degrees.
challenging.for: Body warmth stays within about a degree, and blood is kept in a narrow range of acidity.
challenging.against: Warmth is lower early in the morning, higher in the afternoon, raised in fever and changes with age. Some scientists prefer the word allostasis for keeping steady by changing the target.

challenging.claim: We breathe because we need oxygen, so low oxygen is what makes us gasp.
challenging.for: Oxygen is truly needed. At very low oxygen, for example high in the mountains, sensors in the neck arteries do speed up breathing.
challenging.against: In everyday life the urge to breathe comes mostly from carbon dioxide building up. People breathing air with very little oxygen but no extra carbon dioxide may feel no urge at all.

challenging.claim: Eating sugar is what causes diabetes.
challenging.for: People with type 2 diabetes often eat a lot of sugary food, and sugary drinks are linked to a higher risk.
challenging.against: Type 1 diabetes is not caused by eating sugar. Type 2 comes from many causes together, including genes, body weight, how active a person is and food as a whole.

challenging.claim: A fever is the illness itself and should always be brought down at once.
challenging.for: A very high fever can be dangerous, and a fever can make a child feel miserable.
challenging.against: A fever is the body raising its warmth set point, and some studies suggest it helps fight infection. Studies are mixed. Doctors advise seeing a doctor for a baby with a fever, a very high fever or one that lasts.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years doctors knew a sad illness in which people grew thin and thirsty and their urine was sweet. Old Indian medical texts attributed to Sushruta call it madhumeha, honey urine, and say that ants gather where it falls. Nobody knew the cause. In 1889, in Strasbourg, Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering took out a dog's pancreas to see how much fat digestion needs this gland. They thought the pancreas was only a digestive gland. Minkowski tested the dog's urine and found a lot of sugar. (A popular tale says flies crowding round the urine gave the clue, but Minkowski himself said it was not so.) So the pancreas did a second job, steering the sugar in the blood. In 1921, in Toronto, Frederick Banting and Charles Best, in John Macleod's laboratory, made an extract that lowered the sugar of a diabetic dog. James Collip purified it for people. In January 1922 a boy of fourteen, Leonard Thompson, was among the first to be treated, and the first whose recovery became famous.
how_we_found_out.who: Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering, then Frederick Banting, Charles Best, John Macleod and James Collip
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the pancreas was only a gland for digesting food, and had nothing to do with the sugar in the blood.

big_questions.q: The water in the bottle stays at one level while water pours through. Is the level a thing, or something that is happening?
big_questions.hint: Try to hold the level in your hands. What would you be holding?

big_questions.q: When your blood sugar is steady, who is doing the work: you, your pancreas, or the sugar itself?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether you chose any of it.

big_questions.q: Your pupils shrink in a flash, before you know the light is bright. If you did not do it, who did?
big_questions.hint: Think about the word 'you' and which parts it includes.

big_questions.q: A person with type 1 diabetes may wear a sensor and an insulin pump that work as part of one loop with their body. Where does the body end and the machine begin?
big_questions.hint: Count the parts of the loop and ask which are 'you'.

big_questions.q: The people who found insulin sold the patent to their university for one dollar. Why might they have done that, and what would you do?
big_questions.hint: Think about who needs insulin, and who could afford it.

big_questions.q: Is a body that never changes healthier than a body that changes a lot, or is being alive always changing?
big_questions.hint: Think about your pulse during a run and in sleep.

big_questions.q: Deer and tigers in a forest keep each other's numbers in range, with no one in charge. Is the forest a kind of body?
big_questions.hint: Look for the two opposing pushes.

big_questions.q: If every creature's body keeps different things steady at different levels, is there one 'just right', or many?
big_questions.hint: Compare a human, a hen and a lizard.

story.title: The Wire at Thalassery
story.note: Imagined. Devaki and Meenakshi Ammal are made up. Thalassery in Kerala is known as the birthplace of the Indian circus. It is true that a person who has taken insulin and has not eaten can have a very low blood sugar, and that fast sugar helps. A person who is shaking and confused should get help from a grown-up at once.
text: The circus tent at Thalassery smelled of canvas, coconut oil and hot tea. Devaki was ten, and she had been walking the low wire for two years. It hung a hand's width above the sawdust, and she still fell off it almost every day.

Her teacher was Meenakshi Ammal, who was sixty-three. Long ago Ammal had walked a wire thirty feet up, in Kolkata and Colombo, with no net. Now she walked only to show the children. Every day before lunch she took a small steel box from her bag, opened it, and pressed a thin needle into her belly. Devaki had stopped asking about it.
'Stop holding the pole so tight,' Ammal said one morning. 'It is a stick, not a snake. Hold it like a bird.'
'But I must keep still,' said Devaki. 'If I move, I fall.'
Ammal laughed so hard she had to sit down on an upturned bucket. 'Still? Child, nobody is ever still on a wire. Watch my feet.'

She stepped onto the wire and walked. Devaki watched her ankles. They were not still at all. The left foot leaned a little to the left, and a moment later it leaned back. The pole dipped, and rose, and dipped again. It all looked like nothing at all, because every lean was cancelled by a lean the other way.
'When I lean left, I push right,' said Ammal from the wire. 'When I lean right, I push left. A hundred times to cross. I only look still because I never stop.'

For weeks Devaki tried. She clutched the pole until her knuckles went pale. She fixed her eyes on the end of the wire and tried to make her body into a plank. She fell off every time. The harder she tried to be still, the more the wire shook.

On the night of the festival the tent was full. Drums rolled. Devaki's first show was a short crossing, on the low wire in the middle of the ring, between two stools. Halfway across, the lights went out.

The generator had failed. The tent fell into the dark, with only a thin grey line of sky at the door. The crowd gasped. Devaki stopped. Her hands tightened on the pole. Her toes clamped the wire. Her whole body turned into a plank.

The wire began to shake. It shook more, the harder she held on. She felt herself tipping, and she had nowhere to look, and she heard Ammal's voice from somewhere in the dark, not loud: 'Not still. Never still.'

Devaki breathed out. She let her left foot lean. She did not fight it. Then she pushed back, a little, with the right. Then she let the right foot lean, and pushed back with the left. She did not look at the wire. She did not look at anything. She only listened to her ankles, and gave each lean its answer, small and quick, left and right.

It was strange. The more she moved, the quieter the wire became. Step by step, she crossed the ring in the dark, and put her foot on the stool at the far side. A moment later, the generator coughed. The lights came on, and the tent roared.
Devaki looked for Ammal. She was sitting on her bucket at the edge of the ring with her hand on her chest. Her face was grey, and her hands were shaking. Sweat stood on her forehead.
'Sugar,' Ammal whispered. 'Quick. In my bag. The jaggery.'

Devaki ran. She found the brown lump wrapped in paper, broke off a piece and put it in Ammal's hand. Then she held the tea glass to her mouth. For a minute, nobody said anything. Slowly the grey went out of Ammal's face.
'I ate late,' said Ammal at last, 'and the needle did not wait for me. It pushed my sugar down, and nothing was there to push it back up.'
'Your body used to do that?' said Devaki. 'Push it back up?'

'My body used to do both. When I was a girl, I ate a sweet and the sugar in my blood went up, and a little gland pushed it down. I ran all day and it went down, and the same body pushed it up. Two hands, you see. The one that pushes down stopped working when I was twelve. So now I do that push by hand, with the needle. And I have to guess how much.' She sipped her tea. 'Guess too much, and I wobble.'
'Like on the wire,' said Devaki.
'Like the wire,' said Ammal. 'Only I wish I could do the wire without thinking, and the sugar too.' She patted the bucket. 'You did the wire without thinking tonight. Did you notice?'
Devaki had not noticed. She had been doing nothing at all, very hard.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Devaki's turn comes when she stops trying to be still and instead answers each lean with a lean the other way. A steady level is two pushes working all the time. The same is true of blood sugar, where insulin pushes down and glucagon pushes up. Ammal's body lost the push-down, so she supplies it with a needle, and cannot always judge the amount. Low sugar from too much insulin gives shaking, sweating, grey skin and confusion, and sweet food or drink given right away helps if the person is awake. In an emergency, call a doctor.
ask: Why did Devaki fall off the wire more when she held very still?
What did Ammal mean by 'two hands'?
Why did Ammal's sugar fall, and why did jaggery help?
Devaki says she was 'doing nothing at all, very hard'. What did she mean?
Which things in your own body might be like the wire?

games.title: Sugar See-Saw: keep the level in the green
games.context: This is a team game about blood sugar. Event cards push the sugar up or down, and you choose response cards from the pancreas and liver to bring it back to the green squares.

setup.art: A strip of eleven squares numbered 0 to 10, with squares 4 to 6 in green, 3 and 7 in yellow, and a coin as the marker on 5.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the board and put the marker on 5.

setup.art: Two piles of cards, event cards on the left and response cards on the right, and three hearts cut from paper.
setup.caption: 2. Shuffle two piles. Take 3 hearts and 3 response cards.

setup.art: A hand turning over an event card and moving the marker up by three squares, then playing an insulin card.
setup.caption: 3. Read an event, move the marker, play a response.

printables.title: 11 squares in a row, numbered 0 to 10, with squares 4 to 6 coloured green, 3 and 7 yellow and the rest red
24 two-sided event cards: what happens on the front, and why on the back

items.f: You eat two idlis with sambar. Move up 2.
items.b: Idli is mostly starch, which your gut turns into glucose, so the blood sugar rises.

items.f: You drink a glass of sweet lassi. Move up 3.
items.b: Sugar in a drink enters the blood quickly, so the level jumps.

items.f: You eat one laddu. Move up 4.
items.b: A laddu is mostly sugar and fat. The sugar enters the blood fast.

items.f: You eat a bowl of plain curd. Move up 1.
items.b: Curd has a little milk sugar, so the rise is small.

items.f: You eat a plate of rice and dal. Move up 3.
items.b: Rice is mostly starch. It is broken down to glucose, so the level rises.

items.f: You skip breakfast and play for an hour. Move down 2.
items.b: Your muscles use sugar for energy while no new sugar arrives.

items.f: You run in a race. Move down 3.
items.b: Working muscles take in lots of sugar to burn.

items.f: You walk a long way to school. Move down 2.
items.b: A long walk uses sugar steadily.

items.f: You sleep through the night with no food for eight hours. Move down 2.
items.b: Your cells keep using sugar all night, and no new food arrives.

items.f: You sip a sweet lime soda. Move up 3.
items.b: A sweet drink has sugar that is ready to enter the blood quickly.

items.f: You eat one guava. Move up 1.
items.b: A guava has little sugar and a lot of fibre, which slows the rise.

items.f: You eat a big plate of biryani. Move up 4.
items.b: A big meal has a lot of starch, and a large rise follows.

items.f: You play cricket all afternoon. Move down 3.
items.b: Hours of running burn a lot of sugar.

items.f: You feel scared before a test. Move up 2.
items.b: Fear makes your body release adrenaline, a hormone that tells the liver to release sugar.

items.f: You eat a slice of birthday cake. Move up 4.
items.b: Cake is full of sugar, and the level rises fast.

items.f: You eat a handful of peanuts. Move up 1.
items.b: Peanuts have mostly fat and protein, so the sugar rises only a little.

items.f: You dance at a wedding for an hour. Move down 3.
items.b: Dancing uses a lot of sugar, like a race.

items.f: You drink a glass of coconut water. Move up 1.
items.b: Coconut water has a little sugar.

items.f: You have a fever and feel unwell. Move up 2.
items.b: Illness makes your body release stress hormones that raise the sugar level.

items.f: A long bus ride makes you skip lunch. Move down 2.
items.b: With no new food, your cells keep using the sugar in your blood.

items.f: You drink a glass of plain water. Do not move.
items.b: Plain water has no sugar, so the level does not change.

items.f: You eat one banana. Move up 2.
items.b: A banana has natural sugar, so the level rises.

items.f: You swim for an hour. Move down 3.
items.b: Swimming works your whole body and burns sugar quickly.

items.f: You eat a bowl of sprout salad. Move up 1.
items.b: Sprouts have starch and fibre, so the level rises slowly.

items.f: Glucagon, some. Move up 2.

items.f: Glucagon, a lot. Move up 3.
items.b: A large amount of glucagon. The liver releases a lot of sugar, and the level rises fast.

rules: The team plays as one body. The marker is the sugar in the blood. It starts on square 5. The team has 3 hearts together.
Each round, turn over the top event card. Read it out loud. Move the marker as the card says.
Then choose one response card from your hand of 3. Read it out loud and move the marker as the card says. Draw a new response card to have 3 again.
If the marker would go below 0 or above 10, keep it on the end square.
After the response, score the square. Green squares score 2 points. Yellow squares score 1 point. On a red square, lose one heart.
Read the back of the event card and the back of the response card after each round, so everyone learns the reason.
Hard rule, from Round 5: play your response card face down. It takes effect only after the next event card is played.
The game ends after 12 rounds, or when all 3 hearts are lost. You win if you still have a heart at the end.
Playing alone, try to beat your own score. Playing with others, talk about the choice together and take turns picking the card.

flow.do: Set out the board. Put the marker on 5. The team has 3 hearts. Shuffle the event cards in one pile and the response cards in another. Deal 3 response cards to the team.
flow.say: We play as one body. The marker is your blood sugar. The green squares are just right. Put the marker on five. We have three hearts. Everyone gets a look at the three response cards.
flow.kid: Put the marker on 5. You have 3 hearts. Look at your 3 response cards.
flow.parent: The cards, the board and the tokens are printed from this unit. If you have no printer, copy them by hand on small paper slips. Use 12 event cards and the 12 response cards, which is enough for a short game. Use a coin as the marker and cut 3 paper hearts. The pile of event cards is the world. The response cards are what your pancreas and liver can do. With two to four children, take turns reading the event and moving the marker. The team chooses the response together, and the youngest child plays the card.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sugar See-Saw. You set up the board and the cards.

flow.do: Play Round 1. Turn over the top event card and read it aloud. Move the marker as the card says. Then the team chooses one response card and moves the marker again. Count the points for the square.
flow.say: Read the event. Move the marker. Now choose one response card to bring it back towards five. Play it and move the marker. Score two points on green, one point on yellow, and lose a heart on red.
flow.kid: Read an event card. Move the marker. Play one response card. Score.

ask.q: Which response did you choose, and why?
good: The one that pulled the marker back to five.
Insulin, because the sugar went up.
Glucagon, because the sugar went down.

flow.parent: Turn the event card over after the move and read the reason on the back. The reason is part of the game. After a round, draw a new response card so the team has 3 again.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first round and see how a response pulls the level back.

flow.do: Play Rounds 2 to 4 the same way. After each round, read the back of the event card and the back of the response card you played. If the marker goes beyond 0 or 10, keep it on the end square.
flow.say: Keep going for three more rounds. After each one, read the reason on the back of the event card and on the back of your response card.
flow.kid: Play rounds 2, 3 and 4. Read the backs of the cards.
flow.parent: You may notice that holding a big response card for the right moment helps. A big response for a small change overshoots. That is how real loops work.

check.q: Why does the team have both an insulin card and a glucagon card to choose from?
options: So the level can be corrected whether it went too high or too low
To make the game longer
Because insulin does not work alone
check.why: A single control can push only one way. The body has an opposing pair, so it can pull the level back down after a meal, and push it back up after a long walk.

flow.context: In this step, you play more rounds and read why each event and response work as they do.

flow.do: Play Rounds 5 to 8. Now try the hard rule. Place your response card face down. It works only after the next event card is played. Move the marker for the next event first, then reveal and move for the response from before.
flow.say: Now the hard rule. Your response card takes effect one turn late. Play it face down. Move for the next event first, and only then reveal and move for the card you played before.
flow.kid: Hard rule. Your response works one turn late. Play it face down.

ask.q: What happened with the late response?
good: The marker swung past the green squares.
I had to guess what would happen next.
Big cards were risky.

flow.parent: Children find that big responses with a delay overshoot, and that small responses work better. This is the same lesson as Late Warmer-Colder. Real bodies reduce the problem by predicting, so insulin starts before the sugar peaks.
flow.context: In this step, you play with a delay, like a body whose message takes time to arrive.

flow.do: Play Rounds 9 to 12. The game ends after 12 rounds, or when all 3 hearts are lost. Add up the points.
flow.say: Four more rounds. If you lose all three hearts, the game ends there. At the end of round twelve, add your points. Try to beat your own score next time.
flow.kid: Play rounds 9 to 12. Add up your points.
flow.parent: A good score is about 16 or more out of 24. Players can win by finishing with at least one heart. If you play alone, try to beat your own score next time.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the game and count the score.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what they thought, what they saw and why. Ask: what was the hardest event card, and why?
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would work? What did you see? Why was the delay hard? Which event was the hardest?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the level went too far in both directions, so two kinds of response were needed, and that a response that arrived late made the swings worse.
flow.think: What would happen in a game if you had only insulin cards and no glucagon cards?
flow.context: This is the last step of Sugar See-Saw. You say what you found and why.

worksheets.title: Two Pushes Make a Steady Level (core)

items.p: A bottle has a trickle going in at the top and a hole letting water out near the bottom. The water level is flat. Which is true?
opts: The water going out equals the water coming in
No water is moving
The hole is blocked
items.why: A flat level means the flow out matches the flow in. Water is still moving. A blocked hole would make the level keep rising.

items.p: A level stays steady when what comes ____ equals what goes out.
items.why: A steady level is a match between the flow in and the flow out. If more came in, the level would rise.

items.p: A flat line on a chart always means that nothing is happening.
items.why: False. A flat level can hide a lot of work. In the Level Bottle, the level was flat while water poured in and out all the time.

items.p: In the Level Bottle, why did deeper water leak out of the hole faster?
opts: Deeper water presses harder on the hole
The hole gets bigger when the water is deep
Water is lazy when it is shallow
items.why: More water above the hole presses harder, so it squirts out faster. That is why a rising level makes its own push back.

items.p: Match each part of the body to what it does with blood sugar.
pairs: lowers the sugar in the blood
raises the sugar in the blood
the gland that makes both hormones
stores sugar and releases it when needed
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The pancreas makes insulin and glucagon. Insulin tells cells and the liver to take sugar in. Glucagon tells the liver to let sugar out. The liver is the store.

items.p: Sort each event by what it does to the sugar in the blood.
items: sleeping through the night with no food
items.a: as given
items.why: Food and glucagon add sugar to the blood. Working muscles and insulin take sugar out. Adrenaline tells the liver to release sugar.

items.p: Meena, a girl in Class 4 in Kochi, counts 21 beats of her pulse in 15 seconds. How many beats a minute is that?
items.why: 15 seconds is a quarter of a minute, so you need four times as many. 21 times 4 is 84 beats a minute.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Your pupils shrink in bright light. Your hand pulls away from a hot pan. You breathe faster after a run. You decide to read a book.
items.a: Deciding to read a book, because it is a choice. The other three happen automatically.
items.why: Pupils, pulling away and faster breathing are fast loops that run without a decision. Reading is a decision.

items.p: Put these in the right order, for what happens when you run.
a: Your muscles use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide
Sensors in the brainstem notice the extra carbon dioxide
Your breathing and pulse speed up
The extra carbon dioxide is breathed out
items.why: Working muscles make more carbon dioxide. Sensors notice, and send a signal that speeds breathing and heart. Breathing out then clears the carbon dioxide.

items.p: In Late Warmer-Colder, players walked past the coin when the calls came late. Explain why.
items.a: The late call told them about where they were a few seconds before, not where they were now. By the time they heard 'warmer', they had already gone past the coin.
items.why: A strong answer says the message was out of date. A correction based on old news goes past the target.

items.p: Draw a see-saw. Write insulin at one end and glucagon at the other. Draw a small ball near the middle for the sugar level.
items.a: A see-saw with insulin labelled on the end pushing down, glucagon on the other end pushing up, and a ball near the middle.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two opposite pushes and the level in between. The ball stays near the middle because both pushes are working.

items.p: What goes wrong in type 1 diabetes?
opts: The body makes almost no insulin
The body makes too much glucagon
The body cannot digest food
items.why: In type 1 diabetes the cells that make insulin are destroyed, so almost no insulin is made. People take insulin from outside.

items.p: Anita and Karthik are looking at a flat line of sugar readings from a healthy child.

views.who: Anita, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The line is flat, so the body is doing nothing. It is resting.

views.who: Karthik, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The line is flat because two things are working hard against each other all the time.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What did you see in this unit that supports it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence, such as the Level Bottle staying flat while water flowed, or the ankle wobbling to stay up.
items.why: Karthik's view matches the evidence. A flat line can hide two opposite pushes. Anita's view fits if you think of steady as still.

items.p: Why do you feel the urge to breathe when you hold your breath? Say what builds up in your blood.
items.a: Carbon dioxide builds up in the blood. Sensors in the brainstem notice it and make you feel the urge to breathe.
items.why: A strong answer names carbon dioxide and the brainstem. The urge comes mostly from carbon dioxide and not from lack of oxygen.

items.p: The main signal that tells you to breathe is ____ building up in your blood.
items.why: Your cells make carbon dioxide all the time. When it builds up, sensors tell you to breathe and clear it away.

items.p: You decide to make your pupils smaller when a bright light comes on.
items.why: False. The pupil light reflex runs through the brainstem in under a second, without any decision.

items.p: A bottle with a hole and a trickle has a steady level of 6 centimetres. The trickle becomes twice as fast. What will the steady level do?
opts: Rise to a new, higher steady level
Stay at 6 centimetres
Fall
items.why: A faster trickle puts in more water, so the level rises until the leak is faster too. The leak grows with depth, so the level stops at a new higher place.

items.p: Water enters a bottle at 5 millilitres a second and leaves the hole at 3 millilitres a second. How many millilitres are added to the water in the bottle in 10 seconds?
items.why: 5 take away 3 is 2 millilitres more coming in than going out each second. In 10 seconds that is 2 times 10, which is 20 millilitres.

items.p: In the Level Bottle, the level rose quickly at first and then more slowly as it came near its steady level. Explain why.
items.a: At first the bottle was shallow, so the leak was small and most of the water stayed in. As the level rose, the leak grew. The gap between water in and water out got smaller, so the level rose more slowly until the two matched.
items.why: A strong answer says the leak grows as the level rises, so the difference between flow in and flow out shrinks.

items.p: After a long gap between meals, which hormone rises?
opts: Glucagon
Insulin
Adrenaline only
items.why: When the blood sugar starts to fall, alpha cells in the pancreas release glucagon. It tells the liver to release stored sugar.

items.p: Insulin tells the liver to release sugar into the blood.
items.why: False. Insulin tells cells to take sugar in and the liver to store it. Glucagon tells the liver to release sugar.

items.p: Match each part to its job.
pairs: notice carbon dioxide in the blood
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are all sensors or controls in loops. The two sets of muscles in the iris form an opposing pair, and so do the two sides of the guard cells' pore.

items.p: Sort each loop by whether it pushes back against a change or pushes the change on.
items: the water level in the Level Bottle
platelets calling more platelets at a cut
a microphone squealing near its speaker
a nerve cell firing a signal
items.a: as given
items.why: Most loops in the body push back, which keeps a level steady. A few push the change on, such as sealing a cut or sending a nerve signal, and something stops them after.

items.p: Rahul's pulse at rest is 72 beats a minute. Just after he stops running it is 140. Two minutes later it is 100. By how many beats a minute did it fall in those two minutes, and how many beats is it still above rest?
items.a: 40 beats a minute fewer. It is still 28 above rest.
items.why: 140 take away 100 is 40. And 100 take away 72 is 28, so the pulse is still 28 above rest.

items.p: Why does a shower swing from too hot to too cold when the hot water is slow to arrive?
opts: You keep correcting before the last correction has arrived
The tap is broken
Hot water is heavier than cold water
items.why: Nothing changes at first, so you turn the tap more. When the first change arrives, you have already turned too far. Late news causes overshoot.

items.p: Zoya says, 'Diabetes happens because a person ate too many sweets.' Give two reasons this is not the whole story.
items.a: Type 1 diabetes happens when the body's own defences destroy the cells that make insulin, which has nothing to do with sweets. Type 2 comes from many causes together, such as genes, body weight and how active a person is.
items.why: A strong answer separates the two types and says that many causes work together. It does not blame the person.

items.p: Draw a graph of pulse against time, from rest, through a run, to recovery. Mark the steepest part of the recovery.
items.a: A line that starts low, rises steeply during the run, falls steeply in the first minute after, then falls more slowly back to the starting level. The steepest fall is just after stopping.
items.why: The pulse falls fastest just after stopping, when the gap from rest is biggest. This matches the water level coming back fastest right after a big push.

items.p: A muscle can only ____, never push. So an arm needs a pair of muscles.
items.why: Because a muscle can only pull, the body has one muscle to pull a bone one way and another to pull it back.

items.p: Priya and Imran are talking about a normal body temperature.

views.who: Priya, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Normal is exactly 37 degrees. Anything else means something is wrong.

views.who: Imran, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Normal moves through the day and in a fever. The body changes its target on purpose.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you check to find out?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and says what it would measure, such as taking the temperature of several people at different times of the day.
items.why: Body warmth does vary with the time of day, and in a fever the brain raises the set point. Imran's view fits the evidence better, though 37 degrees is a useful average.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? The level in the Level Bottle, the blood sugar of a healthy child, a wobbling ankle on one leg, a stone on the table.
items.a: The stone, because nothing flows in or out of it and nothing is correcting it. The other three stay steady through constant movement.
items.why: A stone stays still because nothing is pushing it. The other three stay steady because two flows or two pushes balance.

items.p: Put these in the right order, for a shower that swings.
a: The water is too cold, so you turn the tap to hot
Nothing changes yet, so you turn the tap more
The hot water arrives, far too hot
You turn the tap back too far, and it is cold again
items.why: The delay makes you correct twice before the first correction arrives. Then you correct too much the other way.

items.p: A doctor shines a small lamp into an injured person's eyes. What is the doctor checking?
opts: That the pupil light reflex, and so the brainstem, is working
That the person can see colours
That the person is not tired
items.why: The pupil light reflex runs through the brainstem. If the pupils do not react, the brainstem may be injured.

items.p: A girl runs a long race. Use insulin and glucagon to explain what her body does with her blood sugar during the race and just after she eats a banana.
items.a: During the race her muscles take in a lot of sugar, so her blood sugar starts to fall. Glucagon rises and tells the liver to release stored sugar, so the level stays near right. When she eats a banana the sugar rises, and the pancreas releases insulin, which tells cells and the liver to take sugar in and store it.
items.why: A strong answer uses both hormones in the right direction, and says that the aim of both is to keep the level steady.

items.p: A person with type 1 diabetes takes insulin and then does not eat for hours. What is most likely?
opts: Their blood sugar falls too low, and they need sugar quickly
Their blood sugar goes very high
Nothing changes
items.why: The insulin keeps lowering the sugar, and no food is adding any. Low sugar causes shaking, sweating and confusion, and fast sugar helps. A grown-up or doctor should be called.

items.p: A can of juice has 24 grams of sugar. A level teaspoon holds 4 grams, and a grown-up has about one teaspoon of sugar in all their blood. How many times more sugar is in the juice than in all the blood?
items.why: 24 divided by 4 is 6 teaspoons. So the can holds about six times the sugar in all the blood, and the body moves it out of the blood so the level stays small.

items.p: The people who found insulin sold their patent to a university for one dollar, so that no company would own it.

views.who: Aisha, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A medicine that keeps people alive should belong to everyone. They were right to sell it for a dollar.

views.who: Rohit, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Making medicine costs money. Someone has to be paid, or it will not be made at all.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you want to know before you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, and asks about cost, who needs the medicine and who can afford it.
items.why: Both views have a point. Insulin saves lives, and making it takes money. The question is how to make sure everyone who needs it can get it.

items.p: Why is it dangerous to take lots of big breaths before holding your breath in water?
opts: Big breaths blow away carbon dioxide, so the urge to breathe comes late and you can faint before you feel it
Big breaths make the water cold
Big breaths make the lungs smaller
items.why: The urge to breathe comes mostly from carbon dioxide. If you blow it off with big breaths, the warning comes late, and oxygen may run out first. Never do it in water.

items.p: A loop with a delay always overshoots, however gently it corrects.
items.why: False. Gentle, small corrections give the message time to arrive. The body also predicts, so it can start a correction before the change arrives.

items.p: A driver steers a car in thick fog and swerves left and right. Use the idea of delay to explain why.
items.a: In fog the driver sees the road late, so they correct for where the car was a moment ago. They steer too far, then too far the other way, like walking past the coin in Late Warmer-Colder.
items.why: A strong answer says that the news is late, and a correction based on old news overshoots.

items.p: Sort each pair by whether the two work against each other like an opposing pair.
items: the muscle that bends the elbow and the muscle that straightens it
the ring and spoke muscles of the iris
items.a: as given
items.why: An opposing pair has two controls that push in opposite directions on the same level. The stomach and heart do different jobs and do not push against each other.

items.p: The Sun stays almost the same size for billions of years. Which explanation fits the idea of this unit?
opts: Gravity pulls inwards and the pressure of hot gas pushes outwards, and the two are equal
The Sun is simply not moving
The Sun has no energy flowing through it
items.why: A star holds steady because two opposite pushes balance. If it shrank, the pressure would rise and push it back out. If it swelled, gravity would pull it back in.

items.p: Draw the Level Bottle when the level is steady. Draw an arrow for the water going in, an arrow for the water going out, and show how long each one is.
items.a: A bottle with a hole near the base, a trickle entering at the top, an arrow in and an arrow out, both the same length.
items.why: When the level is steady, the flow in equals the flow out, so the two arrows must be the same length.

items.p: The pupil light reflex runs through a part of the brain called the ____.
items.why: Signals from the eye go to the brainstem, which sends a message back to the iris muscles. This is why doctors can use it to check the brainstem.

items.p: Tara breathes 20 times a minute at rest. How many breaths does she take in one hour, and how many in a whole day?
items.a: 1,200 in an hour and 28,800 in a day.
items.why: 20 times 60 is 1,200 breaths in an hour. 1,200 times 24 is 28,800 breaths in a day.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found out.
pairs: worked out the shape of the insulin molecule
helped show with Solomon Berson that many adults with diabetes have insulin that works poorly
made an extract that lowered the blood sugar of diabetic dogs
Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering
found that taking out a dog's pancreas caused diabetes
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of them added a piece. It took many people over decades to understand diabetes and to treat it.

items.p: Give a new example, not from this unit, of something that stays steady because two opposite pushes balance. Say what the two pushes are.
items.a: A person riding a bicycle: they lean left and steer right, then lean right and steer left. Or a hanging mobile, a swing at rest, or a floating boat. The answer must name two opposite pushes.
items.why: A strong answer names two pushes in opposite directions that keep a level or a position steady.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? The Level Bottle, a room thermostat, a pressure cooker whistle, a microphone squealing near its speaker.
items.a: The microphone, because the louder sound makes it louder still. The others push back against a change.
items.why: The microphone is positive feedback, which pushes the change on. The other three are negative feedback, which pushes back.

experiments.title: Level Bottle: a bottle that keeps its own water level
experiments.question: Water trickles into a bottle with a small hole near the bottom. Does the level keep rising, or does it stop? What happens to the level if the trickle gets faster?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the water level keep rising, or stop? Will a faster trickle change where it stops? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same bottle and the same hole are used every time. The ruler stays in the same place. The trickle falls in the same spot. You read the level every 15 seconds, until two readings in a row match. Only the speed of the trickle changes, so any difference in the steady level comes from the speed.
results_table: Steady level when two readings in a row match (centimetres above the hole)

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle, about 1 litre, with the top cut off at the shoulder by a grown-up
a compass point or a sharp pin for the hole, used by a grown-up (a fine nail also works)
a ruler and some tape
a cup or tumbler marked in millilitres. If yours has no marks, mark it with a pen: 4 medicine spoons of 5 millilitres make 20 millilitres
a clock with seconds, or a phone timer (a stopwatch is not needed)
a kitchen sink with a tap, and a towel
the results table and a pencil
scissors or a knife for cutting the bottle, and tape to cover the sharp cut edge, used by a grown-up
a spare bottle, in case the first hole comes out too wide

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottle and makes the hole, because the scissors and the point are sharp. Cover the cut edge with tape. Wipe up spills so nobody slips.
experiments.record: Write the steady level for each trickle speed. Then say, in one sentence, why the level stops. If a test goes over the rim or never settles, write that down as it is and use a slower trickle. If the level stays under 1 centimetre even with the fastest trickle, the hole is too big: use the spare bottle.
experiments.context: In this experiment you build a bottle that keeps its own water level, and find out what decides where the level stops.

setup.art: A clear bottle with its top cut off, a small hole near the base, a ruler taped on the side with zero at the hole.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes the hole. Tape a ruler on with zero at the hole.

setup.art: A cup under a thin tap trickle with a clock, showing 20 millilitres in 10 seconds.
setup.caption: 2. Catch the trickle in a cup for 10 seconds. Aim for about 20 millilitres.

setup.art: The bottle in a sink with a thin trickle entering at the top and a jet leaving the hole, level line marked.
setup.caption: 3. Let the trickle fall into the bottle. Watch the level.

setup.art: A child reading the level on the taped ruler at eye height, a note pad beside the sink.
setup.caption: 4. Read the level every 15 seconds until two readings match.

setup.art: A hand pouring a cup of water quickly into the bottle, with the level jumping up and then a dotted arrow showing it coming back down.
setup.caption: 5. Pour in a cupful quickly and watch the level come back.

flow.do: Show your child a clear bottle with a small hole near the bottom, standing in the sink. Open the tap to a thin trickle. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Water will trickle in from the top and leak out of this hole. What will the water level do? Will it rise until the bottle overflows, or will it stop? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Water trickles in and leaks out of the hole. Will the level keep rising or stop? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think it will do that?
good: The hole lets water out.
The water will run out as fast as it comes in.
It will fill up because the tap is stronger.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Both 'it will overflow' and 'it will stop' are good guesses if there is a reason. Write the guess and the reason at the top of the results table. With two to four children, each one makes their own guess and the pairs share the roles: one holds the tap, one reads the ruler, one writes, one times. Rotate the jobs for each trickle speed. Make one bottle for each pair if you can.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Level Bottle test. You guess before you look.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the top off the bottle at the shoulder. Then they push a compass point through the side, 2 centimetres above the base. Twist it until the hole is just wide enough for a ballpoint refill. Tape a ruler beside the hole with zero at the hole.
flow.say: A grown-up must make the hole, because the point is sharp. The hole should be just wide enough for a pen refill to slide in. The ruler's zero must be at the hole, so we measure the level above the hole.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes the hole. Tape the ruler beside it. Put zero at the hole.
flow.parent: Use the same bottle and the same hole for every test. A hole much wider than a ballpoint refill leaks too fast for a thin tap trickle to ever fill it. If the hole is too big, use the spare bottle. Do not try to tape over a wet bottle. The hole of a compass point is usually about 2 to 3 millimetres, which suits a tap trickle of about 20 to 40 millilitres in 10 seconds.

check.q: Why must we use the same bottle and the same hole for every test?
options: So that only the speed of the trickle changes
So the bottle looks tidy
So the water is cleaner
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the hole changed too, you would not know whether the trickle or the hole made the level different.

flow.context: In this step, you build the Level Bottle. The ruler tells you how high the water stands above the hole.

flow.do: Hold a cup under the tap. Open the tap until the trickle fills about 20 millilitres in 10 seconds. Mark that tap position with a bit of tape.
flow.say: Catch the trickle in a cup for ten seconds. Aim for about 20 millilitres. That is a very thin trickle. Mark the tap so you can find that spot again.
flow.kid: Catch the trickle in a cup for ten seconds. Aim for about 20 millilitres.
flow.parent: Tap pressure changes during the day, and a thin trickle is hard to hold steady. If the tap is too strong to trickle, run it into a jug and pour from a mug instead. If your cup has no marks, use a medicine measuring cup. The numbers are a guide. What matters is that each setting stays the same during its test.
flow.context: In this step, you measure how fast the tap trickles. This is the speed of the water going in.

flow.do: Set the bottle in the sink, empty. Let the trickle fall into the middle of the bottle. Read the level every 15 seconds and write it down. Stop when two readings in a row match, or after 3 minutes.
flow.say: Watch the level. Read it every fifteen seconds. Is it still rising? Where does it stop? Stop when two readings in a row match.
flow.kid: Read the level every 15 seconds. Does it stop rising?

ask.q: Water keeps pouring in. Why does the level stop?
good: The water leaves as fast as it comes in.
The hole lets out as much as the tap gives.
The deeper water pushes more out of the hole.

flow.parent: The level should rise quickly at first, then slow down, then stay put. It can take 2 to 4 minutes to settle, because the bottle is wide and the trickle is thin. The steady level for a thin trickle is often only a few centimetres, but your hole and tap will give different numbers. Write what you see. Do not empty the bottle before the next test.

check.q: The level stopped rising, but the tap is still running. What must be true?
options: Water leaves the hole as fast as it comes in
The tap has stopped
The hole has closed
check.why: If the level is flat, the water going out equals the water coming in. A flat level does not mean water has stopped moving. It means both flows match.

flow.context: In this step, you run the first test with the slowest trickle and watch the level.

flow.do: Do not empty the bottle. Open the tap to about 30 millilitres in 10 seconds. Read every 15 seconds until two readings in a row match. Then do about 40 millilitres in 10 seconds. Write each steady level in the table.
flow.say: Now make the trickle faster. First about thirty millilitres in ten seconds. Read the level until it stops changing. Then about forty. What happens to the steady level each time?
flow.kid: Make the trickle faster. Read until the level stops. Write the steady level.

ask.q: Why does a faster trickle give a higher steady level?
good: The water has to be deeper to leak out faster.
More water needs more push to get out of the hole.
The level rises until the leak matches the trickle.

flow.parent: The steady level should rise each time the trickle gets faster, and by more than you might expect. In theory, a trickle twice as fast raises the steady level to about four times as high. Real bottles give less than that, so do not promise the number. If the water goes over the rim, the trickle is too fast for your hole. Note it and use a slower trickle. Each new setting needs 2 to 3 minutes to settle.
flow.context: In this step, you change only one thing, the speed of the trickle, and see where the level settles.

flow.do: With the level steady at the 30 millilitre setting, tip in a cupful of water all at once. Watch the level every 10 seconds. Does it stay high, or come back?
flow.say: Now give the bottle a shock. Pour in a cup of water quickly. What does the level do? Does it stay high, or come back to the old level?
flow.kid: Pour a cup in quickly. Does the level stay high or come back?

ask.q: Why does the level come back down?
good: The water is deeper, so it leaks out faster.
The bigger the change, the faster the leak.
The extra water pushes itself out.

flow.parent: The level jumps up, then falls quickly at first and more slowly, and comes back to near the same steady level. The further away it was pushed, the faster it came back. That is negative feedback. If the water goes over the rim, use half a cup.

check.q: Why does the leak get faster when the water is deeper?
options: Deeper water pushes harder on the hole
The hole gets bigger
The water wants to leave
check.why: The deeper the water, the more it presses on the hole, so it squirts out faster. The level itself drives the leak, so a change causes its own push back.

flow.context: In this step, you push the level away from its steady place and see whether it comes back.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what they thought, what they saw, and why it happened. Write their answer under the table.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did the level stop, and why did it come back after the shock?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why the level stopped.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the level stops where the water going out matches the water coming in, and that deeper water leaks faster, which is why the level comes back. Only after they have said this, explain: the level works as its own sensor. The higher it rises, the faster it leaks. Your body's sugar works like this. The higher the sugar, the more insulin pushes it back down.
flow.think: Your blood sugar is like this level. What do you think does the job of the hole?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Level Bottle test. You say what you found and why.

experiments.title: Recovery Race: how fast do my pulse and breathing come back?
experiments.question: After exercise, how long does it take for my pulse and breathing to come back to rest? Does a harder effort take longer?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How long will your pulse take to come back to rest after one minute of stepping? Will two minutes of marching take twice as long? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same child, the same clock and the same way of finding the pulse are used each time. The rest period before each try is long enough for the pulse to return to normal. Only the exercise changes, one minute of stepping and then two minutes of marching.
results_table: Breaths in 30 seconds (counted by a helper)

materials.item: a low stool or the bottom stair, on a floor that does not slip
a clock with seconds, or a phone timer
a chair to sit on
a helper to count breaths and keep time (a brother, sister or friend can do this)
a glass of water
the results table and a pencil
a pen and a sheet of paper to copy the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays with the child the whole time. Do not do the test if your child is unwell or has been told to avoid exercise. Stop if they feel dizzy or have chest pain. Keep an inhaler close for a child with asthma. Never hold the breath in water, and never take big breaths first.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then mark the biggest drop in pulse and the minute in which it came. Say in one sentence which try took longer to come back and by how much. If the numbers jump about, that is real. Counting a pulse for 15 seconds is only accurate to a few beats.
experiments.context: In this experiment you race your pulse and breathing back to rest after exercise, and see how the return happens.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair with two fingers on the inside of the wrist and a helper holding a clock.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still for 3 minutes. Find your pulse and count for 15 seconds.

setup.art: A child holding a normal breath with a finger on the nose bridge and a helper with a clock, standing on dry floor.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a normal breath until the first strong urge. Not in water.

setup.art: A child stepping onto a low stool, with an adult standing beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Step up and down on the stool for one minute.

setup.art: A child sitting, fingers on the wrist, helper counting breaths from the shoulders and a table with counts.
setup.caption: 4. Sit down and count the pulse every minute for 4 minutes.

setup.art: A child marching on the spot with knees high, an adult beside them, a clock on the wall.
setup.caption: 5. After a rest, march for 2 minutes and count again.

flow.do: Show your child the low stool, the clock and the table. Say that they will race their pulse back to rest after one minute of stepping, then after two minutes of marching. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: After one minute of stepping, how long will your pulse take to come back to rest? Will two minutes of marching take twice as long? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: After a minute of stepping, how long until your pulse is back to rest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think it will take that long?
good: My heart has to slow down.
I was working harder.
My body needs time to catch up.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Do not do this test if your child is unwell, or if a doctor has said to avoid exercise. A child with asthma should have an inhaler close by. With two to four children, work in pairs. One steps, one counts the pulse, one counts breaths, one keeps time. Each child does the stepping in turn, while the others rest. Allow extra time, and compare the recovery times across children.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Recovery Race. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Sit your child on a chair for 2 minutes. Show them how to find the pulse: two fingers on the inside of the wrist, below the thumb. Count the beats for 15 seconds, twice. Multiply the second count by 4. Count their breaths for 30 seconds too.
flow.say: Sit quietly for two minutes. Find your pulse with two fingers below your thumb. Count for fifteen seconds. I will count your breaths, one in and one out. Write both down as your resting numbers.
flow.kid: Sit quietly. Find your pulse. Count beats for 15 seconds.
flow.parent: Use two fingers, not the thumb, because the thumb has a pulse of its own. If the wrist pulse is hard to find, lay a flat hand on the left side of the chest, or on the side of the neck under the jaw, lightly. Practise at rest first. Resting pulse for most children of 6 to 10 is about 70 to 110 beats a minute, and breathing about 16 to 25 breaths a minute. Your child may be different, and that is fine. Count the breaths by watching the shoulders or belly.

check.q: Why do we count the pulse for 15 seconds and then multiply by 4?
options: It gives beats in a whole minute, without waiting a whole minute
It makes the pulse slower
It makes the count more exciting
check.why: 15 seconds is a quarter of a minute, so the count times 4 gives the beats in one minute. It is faster than counting for a full minute, and the pulse is still steady enough to count.
