flow.context: In this step, you measure your resting pulse and breathing, so you know your own normal.

flow.do: Ask your child to hold a normal breath, not a big one, and not to take any deep breaths first. Time how long until the first strong urge to breathe. Then they breathe out and breathe normally. Write down the seconds. Do this only once.
flow.say: Take a normal breath, not a big one. Hold it. Tell me the moment you feel a strong urge to breathe. Then breathe out. Not before, and never a deep breath first.
flow.kid: Take a normal breath and hold it. Stop at the first strong urge.
flow.parent: Never do breath-holding in water, and never take big breaths first, because that hides the urge and can lead to fainting. Stop at the first strong urge. Many children reach 20 to 40 seconds, but the number is not a score. Skip this part if your child dislikes it or has asthma or a breathing problem.

check.q: Why do we stop at the first strong urge to breathe?
options: The urge is a warning from your body, and we respect it
The test is finished only then
The urge means we are cheating
check.why: The urge is a signal from your brainstem that carbon dioxide has built up. Respecting it keeps the test safe. Pushing past it, and especially taking big breaths first, can lead to fainting.

flow.context: In this step, you time how long you can hold your breath before the urge to breathe comes. Never do this in water.

flow.do: Try 1. Your child steps up on the low stool and down again for one minute. The pace is steady, about one step up and down every two seconds. A grown-up stands next to them. Then they sit at once.
flow.say: Step up onto the stool and down again, nice and steady, for one minute. I will tell you when to stop. Then sit down straight away.
flow.kid: Step up and down on the stool for one minute. Then sit.
flow.parent: Stop at once if your child feels dizzy, has pain in the chest, or is much more breathless than seems right. Keep a hand near them. Use the bottom stair or a stool that does not slip.
flow.context: In this step, you push your pulse and breathing up with one minute of stepping.

flow.do: As soon as your child sits, start the clock. Count their pulse for 15 seconds at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 minutes after stopping. Count their breaths for 30 seconds at 0 and 2 minutes. After the 1 minute pulse count, time one breath-hold, stopping at the first urge.
flow.say: Sit down and keep still. Count your pulse for fifteen seconds right now. Do it again at one minute, two, three and four. After the one minute count, hold a normal breath until the first urge.
flow.kid: Sit. Count your pulse for 15 seconds, at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 minutes.

ask.q: What is happening to your breathing and pulse as the minutes pass?
good: They are slowing down.
They are coming back to rest.
My body is catching its breath.

flow.parent: The pulse is highest right at the start and falls quickly in the first minute. After that it falls more slowly. It may take 2 to 5 minutes to reach rest. A breath-hold after exercise is usually shorter than at rest, because carbon dioxide is still high. Offer this only if your child is comfortable, and skip it in Try 2.
flow.context: In this step, you measure how your pulse and breathing come back to rest after Try 1.

flow.do: Let your child rest until their pulse is back to their resting number, usually 3 to 5 minutes. Then Try 2: march on the spot with knees high for 2 minutes. Sit at once. Count the pulse at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 minutes, as before.
flow.say: Rest until your pulse is back to your resting number. Then march on the spot with your knees high for two whole minutes. Sit down and we measure the pulse again.
flow.kid: Rest. Then march on the spot for two minutes. Sit and measure again.
flow.parent: If your child is tired, make Try 2 shorter, about 90 seconds, and write what they did. The question is whether a harder effort needs longer to recover. Keep the same counting times as in Try 1. Use the resting time to fill in the table. If the pulse does not come back to the resting number within 6 minutes, write that down and stop for the day.
flow.context: In this step, you do a harder Try 2 and measure the recovery again.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what they thought, what they saw, and why. Ask them to find the biggest drop in pulse in the table, and in which minute it came.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see in the numbers? Why did your breathing and pulse come back down?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the pulse and breathing rose when the muscles worked, and fell after they stopped, with the biggest fall in the first minute. Only after they have said it, explain: working muscles make more carbon dioxide. Sensors in the brainstem notice this and speed up breathing and the heart. When you stop, the carbon dioxide is cleared and the speed falls. Like the water level in the bottle, the further the level was pushed, the faster it came back at first.
flow.think: The urge to breathe came sooner after the stepping. What do you think was different in your blood?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Recovery Race. You say what you found and why.

experiments.title: Pupil Gauge: how fast do my pupils fix the light?
experiments.question: When the light changes, how fast and how far does the pupil change? Is it something I decide?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When a lamp comes on, will the pupil change slowly or fast? Will it get bigger or smaller? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same child, the same lamp at the same distance, and the same 2 minutes in the dim room are used each time. The child always looks at the same spot on the wall. Only the light changes, from dim to lamp on and back to dim.

materials.item: a strip of white card, a fine black pen and a ruler
an ordinary room lamp that can be switched on and off
a clock with seconds, or a phone timer
a phone to film the eye from the side, with the gauge beside it (no flash)
a helper
the results table and a pencil
a small mirror, if you have one, for the child to watch their own eye

experiments.safety: Never shine a torch, a phone flash or any bright light straight into anyone's eyes. The lamp stays at the side of the face, and the child looks at the wall. Do the test no more than three times.
experiments.record: Write the pupil size at each moment. Then write whether the pupil changed quickly or slowly, and whether you decided to change it. If very dark eyes made the pupil hard to see, write that and film the face to read it later, or use the cover test in step 4 and write small, medium or large.
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a gauge for the black dot in the eye, and watch it change when the light comes on and goes off.

setup.art: A strip of white card with six black dots of growing size, numbered 2 to 7, and a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw six black dots, 2 to 7 millimetres wide, on a card strip.

setup.art: A dim room with closed curtains, a child sitting and looking at a spot on the wall, and a lamp switched off beside their face.
setup.caption: 2. Make the room dim. Sit for 2 minutes and look at a spot on the wall.

setup.art: A helper holding the gauge beside the child's cheek with a lamp switched on at the side, 40 centimetres away.
setup.caption: 3. The lamp goes on. The helper reads the pupil against the gauge.

setup.art: A phone on a stand filming a close-up of an eye, with a pause button visible on the screen.
setup.caption: 4. If it is too fast to read, film the face and pause the film.

flow.do: Show your child their eyes in a mirror. Ask for a guess and a reason. When the lamp comes on after a dim minute, how fast will the black dot change, and how far?
flow.say: Look at the black dot in the middle of your eye. When the light comes on after a dim minute, will it change slowly or fast? Will it get bigger or smaller? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the black dot in your eye. When light comes on, what will it do? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think it will do that?
good: Bright light hurts, so it closes.
It lets in less light.
It gets smaller to protect the eye.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children say it will change slowly. The real change is very fast. With two to four children, each guesses first. Then they take turns as the eye, the gauge reader, the lamp switcher and the timekeeper.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pupil Gauge test. You guess before you look.

flow.do: Cut a strip of white card. Use a ruler to draw six black filled circles on it, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 millimetres wide. Write the number under each. This is the pupil gauge.
flow.say: Cut a strip of white card. Draw six black dots in a row. Make them two, three, four, five, six and seven millimetres wide. Check each one with the ruler. Write its size under it.
flow.kid: Draw six black dots on a card strip. Make them 2 to 7 millimetres wide.
flow.parent: The dots need not be perfect, but they must be about the right size. A bottle cap is too big. Use a fine black pen and check across each dot with the ruler. In a dim room a child's pupil can be bigger than 7 millimetres, so write 'bigger than 7' if it is. Very dark brown eyes make the pupil hard to see against the iris. A bright lamp from the side, or a pale-eyed helper, makes it easier.
flow.context: In this step, you make a pupil gauge to read the size of a pupil, the way a ruler reads a length.

flow.do: Close the curtains and switch off the room lights, until the room is dim but you can still see each other. Put a lamp, switched off, 40 centimetres to the side of your child's face. Your child looks at a spot on the wall for 2 minutes.
flow.say: Now we make the room dim. Close the curtains and switch off the lights. Put the lamp beside your face, switched off. Sit and look at one spot on the wall for two minutes.
flow.kid: Make the room dim. Sit for two minutes. Look at a spot on the wall.
flow.parent: The lamp must be to the side, never shone straight into the eyes. Use an ordinary room lamp, not a torch or a phone flash. Keep a little light, such as a dim passage light, so the pupil can be seen. In the dim room the helper holds the gauge against the cheekbone and reads the pupil as best they can. Write the size at 2 minutes. Pupils keep opening for about 20 minutes, so 2 minutes is a fair start, not the full dark.
flow.context: In this step, you let your pupils open in the dim room. This is your starting level.

flow.do: Your child keeps looking at the wall spot. The helper switches the lamp on. Film the eye with the gauge beside it. Then pause the film at 1 second, 5 seconds and 30 seconds, and read the pupil.
flow.say: Keep looking at the wall spot. I will switch the lamp on and film your eye. Afterwards I pause the film at one second, five seconds and thirty seconds. I read your pupil against the gauge.
flow.kid: Look at the spot. The lamp goes on. We read your pupil size.

ask.q: What did the pupil do when the light came on?
good: It got smaller very fast.
It shrank and then got a little bigger.
It changed before I could decide anything.

flow.parent: Most children's pupils shrink in well under a second, and some then widen a little and settle within about 10 seconds. Reading a pupil by eye in one second is hard, so the film is the main method. Easier version without a lamp, in an ordinary lit room: the child covers one eye with a palm for 30 seconds, then uncovers it. Watch that pupil shrink within a second, and compare it with the other eye. Both pupils shrink, because they work as a pair. If your child blinks or looks away, repeat after 2 minutes in the dim room. Never repeat more than three times.

check.q: Why do we ask your child to look at a spot on the wall and not at the lamp?
options: So the lamp is not shone into the eyes, and the eye stays in one place to read
So the lamp looks nicer
So the light stays away from the wall
check.why: A steady gaze lets the helper read the pupil. And looking at the wall keeps the light at the side. Looking straight at a bright light is uncomfortable and not good for the eyes.

flow.context: In this step, you switch the light on and read how the pupil changes in the first seconds.

flow.do: Now switch the lamp off and ask your child to keep looking at the wall spot. Film again. Read the pupil at 5 seconds, 30 seconds and 60 seconds after the lamp goes off.
flow.say: Now the lamp goes off. Keep looking at the spot. I read your pupil at five seconds, thirty seconds and one minute. Does it open as fast as it closed?
flow.kid: The lamp goes off. We read your pupil again at three times.
flow.parent: Opening in the dark is slower than closing in the light. It continues slowly for a minute or more, and the eye's sensitivity keeps improving for about 20 to 30 minutes. This is why a dark cinema seems blacker at first.
flow.context: In this step, you watch your pupils open again when the light goes away.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what they thought, what they saw, and why. Ask: did they decide to change their pupils?
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see on the gauge? Why did your pupils change? Did you decide to do it?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the pupil got smaller in the light and bigger in the dark, and changed without being decided. Only after that, explain: light on the back of the eye sends a signal to the brainstem, which tells a ring of tiny muscles to tighten and shrink the pupil. In the dark, a second set of muscles shaped like spokes pulls it wide. Two opposite muscle sets make an opposing pair.
flow.think: If a loop can run in under a second without you, what else in you might be running?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Pupil Gauge test. You say what you found and why.

activities.title: One-Leg Wobble: how still is 'still'?
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity. You stand on one leg and find out what your ankle is doing to keep you up.

materials.item: a wall or a chair to hold, a clear floor, and a folded blanket or cushion for the extra try
a clock with seconds, or a phone timer
a helper (a brother, sister or friend can do this)

activities.record: Write how many shifts your helper counted with your eyes open, and how many with your eyes closed. Write how many seconds you stayed up each time, up to 20. Write one sentence on what your ankle was doing.

setup.art: A child standing on one leg near a wall, arms out, with a helper crouching to watch the standing ankle.
setup.caption: 1. Stand on one leg for 20 seconds. Your helper watches your ankle.

setup.art: The same child with eyes closed, the helper's hand near but not touching, a cushion on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Try 10 seconds with your eyes closed.

setup.art: Two fingers resting on the inside and outside of an ankle, with small arrows showing a pull to one side and then the other.
setup.caption: 3. Your helper feels both sides of the ankle tighten in turn.

flow.do: Ask your child to stand near a wall. Say that they will stand on one leg for 20 seconds. Ask for a guess and a reason: will the standing foot stay still?
flow.say: Stand on one leg for twenty seconds. Will your foot and ankle stay still? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will stand on one leg for 20 seconds. Will your foot stay still? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: I will hold it very still.
My foot will wobble.
I have to keep moving to stay up.

flow.parent: Stand close to the child, or put a hand on the wall for safety. Do it barefoot or in socks with grip, on a floor that does not slip. Do not correct the guess. With two to four children, take turns. While one stands, one counts shifts, one times the seconds and one stays close to catch. Compare the numbers across the group.
flow.context: This is the first step of One-Leg Wobble. You guess before you try.

flow.do: Your child stands on one leg, eyes open, for up to 20 seconds. You count how many times the standing foot and ankle visibly shift, and time how long they stay up. Then they try with eyes closed, for up to 10 seconds, with you right beside them.
flow.say: Stand on one leg and look at one spot. I will watch your ankle and count each shift. Then you will try with your eyes closed, for ten seconds, and I will stay close.
flow.kid: Stand on one leg for 20 seconds. Then 10 seconds with eyes closed.

ask.q: What did your foot and ankle do?
good: They kept moving a little.
My toes gripped the floor.
It was harder with my eyes closed.

flow.parent: Most children shift many times, and more with eyes closed. Keep a hand near. Put a cushion or mat on the floor. Have them stop if they feel unsafe. Try the same with eyes open on a folded blanket. The soft surface makes it harder for the same reason: the feet get less clear signals.

check.q: When you stand on one leg, what is your ankle doing?
options: Making many small corrections, left and right
Staying perfectly still
Resting
check.why: To stay up, your ankle keeps tilting a little and your muscles keep correcting it. Standing still is made of many small movements.

flow.context: In this step, you stand on one leg and your helper counts the shifts of your ankle.

flow.do: Your child stands on one leg again. You rest two fingers lightly on the inside of the ankle and then on the outside. You feel the tendons tighten, one side and then the other.
flow.say: Stand on one leg again. I will rest my fingers on both sides of your ankle. Tell me if you feel it tighten, and which side tightens first.
flow.kid: Stand on one leg. Your helper feels both sides of your ankle.
flow.parent: Place your fingers lightly, just below the ankle bone on each side. The tendons on both sides tighten in turn as the body tilts one way and back. They are small movements, and some children are hard to feel. If they are hard to find, watch the toes grip the floor and the lifted foot wobble. Those are also the correction.
flow.context: In this step, you feel the two sides of the ankle pulling in turn.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what they thought, what they saw and why. Then ask: how can a thing look still when so much is moving?
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why did your ankle keep moving? How can something look still when so much is moving?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the ankle kept tilting and being pulled back, in both directions, to keep standing. Only after that, explain: your brain gets signals from your feet, eyes and inner ears, and sends them to your muscles, which correct each tilt. To stand still, you move all the time.
flow.think: Which other things in your body might look still but be working all the time?
flow.context: This is the last step of One-Leg Wobble. You say what you found and why.

activities.title: One Teaspoon: the sugar in all your blood
activities.context: In this activity you see how little sugar is in the blood, compared with the sugar in food and drinks.

materials.item: about 100 grams of sugar (a small cup) and a flat measuring teaspoon or an ordinary teaspoon
a saucer and a plate
three food or drink packs with nutrition labels, from the kitchen or a kirana shop (a biscuit packet, a juice box and a cola are good)
a kitchen weighing scale, if you have one, to check that a level teaspoon of sugar is about 4 grams (not needed to do the activity)
paper and a pencil
a tray or plate to work on, so spilled sugar can be wiped up at once

activities.record: Write the three foods, the grams of sugar and the teaspoons. Write one sentence on where you think the sugar goes.

setup.art: A level teaspoon being tipped onto a saucer, a small mound of sugar, with a label 'all the sugar in your blood'.
setup.caption: 1. Tip one level teaspoon of sugar onto a saucer.

setup.art: A child reading the sugars line on a drink bottle label and writing the number on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Find the grams of sugar on a label. Write it down.

setup.art: A plate with six small piles of sugar from a teaspoon next to a saucer with one pile and a cola bottle in the middle.
setup.caption: 3. Divide by 4. Spoon that many teaspoons onto the plate.

flow.do: Show your child a small bottle of cola or a packet of biscuits. Say that all the blood in a grown-up holds about one teaspoon of sugar. Ask for a guess and a reason: how many teaspoons of sugar are in a 250 millilitre bottle of cola?
flow.say: All the blood in a grown-up holds about one teaspoon of sugar. How many teaspoons are in a small bottle of cola? Take a guess. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Your blood holds about one teaspoon of sugar. How many are in a small cola? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that many?
good: It tastes very sweet.
Drinks have lots of sugar.
I am not sure, so I will check.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children guess one to three. The label usually says about six. With two to four children, each guesses before anyone checks, and each takes a different pack to measure. Compare at the end.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Teaspoon. You guess before you check.

flow.do: Fill a level teaspoon with sugar and tip it onto a saucer. A level teaspoon of sugar is about 4 grams. Say that this is about all the sugar in the blood of a grown-up.
flow.say: Fill a teaspoon with sugar, level to the top, and tip it onto the saucer. This small pile is about all the sugar that is in a grown-up's blood at one time.
flow.kid: Tip one level teaspoon of sugar onto a saucer. This is all the sugar in your blood.
flow.parent: A child has less blood than a grown-up, so a little less sugar. A level teaspoon of table sugar is about 4 grams. Spoons differ a little, from about 3 to 5 grams, so say 'about'. A healthy grown-up has about 4 to 5 grams of sugar in all of their blood, which is about 5 litres.
flow.context: In this step, you see how small the amount of sugar in the blood is.

flow.do: Find three food or drink packs with a nutrition label. Find the grams of sugar in one serving for each. Divide by 4 to get teaspoons. Spoon that many teaspoons onto a plate.
flow.say: Find three packs with labels. Look for the line that says sugars. Check if it is for one serving or for 100 grams. Divide the grams by four. Spoon that many teaspoons onto a plate.
flow.kid: Find three labels. Write the sugar. Divide by four for teaspoons.

ask.q: What do you notice when you look at the plate beside the saucer?
good: The plate has much more.
The cola has about six times as much.
It is a lot of sugar for one drink.

flow.parent: Watch the label column. Many Indian packs give grams per 100 grams or 100 millilitres, and sometimes also per serving. For a 250 millilitre cola, multiply the 100 millilitre figure by 2.5. It comes to about 26 grams, about 6 teaspoons. If you have no labels, use 26 grams for a 250 millilitre cola. A plain biscuit or a packet of puffed rice has very little sugar, and juice can have a lot. Do not eat the sugar off the plate. Wipe it up at once, because ants come quickly in warm weather. Do not drink the cola for the test, and no food should be wasted.
flow.context: In this step, you turn grams of sugar on a label into teaspoons you can see.

flow.do: Ask your child: the plate of sugar for the cola is about six times the sugar in all your blood. Where did it go after you drank it, and why did your blood sugar not go up six times?
flow.say: The cola holds about six times the sugar in all your blood. If you drank it, your blood sugar would not go up six times. Where do you think the sugar goes? Who moves it?
flow.kid: The cola has six times your blood's sugar. Where does it all go?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that something moves the sugar out of the blood into the cells and the liver. Only after they have said it, explain: insulin tells cells to take the sugar in and the liver to store it. The sugar in the blood is a small amount that is always being moved in and out. It is like the bottle level, where a lot flows through but the level stays small.
flow.think: What would happen to the blood if the sugar kept going in and nothing took it out?
flow.context: This is the last step of One Teaspoon. You think about how the body keeps the amount steady.

activities.title: Push-Pull Pairs: why the body uses two
activities.context: In this activity you feel a pair of muscles pulling against each other, and find other pairs in your body.

materials.item: a sturdy table or desk with a flat underside, to press against
a full water bottle
paper and a pencil for the list

activities.record: Write the list of pairs, and one sentence on why a body might use a pair instead of one control.

setup.art: A child with one hand on the front of the upper arm and the other on the back, elbow bent.
setup.caption: 1. Put one hand on the front and one on the back of your upper arm.

setup.art: A child lowering a full water bottle slowly, both hands feeling the arm muscles.
setup.caption: 2. Press your palm up under the table, then down on top. Feel both muscles.

setup.art: A list on paper titled 'pairs in my body' with sketches of an arm, a drop of sweat, a snowflake and an eye.
setup.caption: 3. Write a list of pairs. Add one of your own.

flow.do: Ask your child to put one hand on the front of the upper arm and the other hand on the back. Ask for a guess and a reason. When they bend the elbow slowly, which muscle will tighten: the front, the back, or both?
flow.say: Put one hand on the front of your upper arm and one on the back. Bend your elbow slowly. Which muscle will tighten, the front or the back? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One hand on the front, one on the back of your arm. Bend slowly. Which tightens?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The one I can see bulging.
Both will work.
The front pulls the arm up.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children say the front muscle only. With two to four children, work in pairs. One feels their own arm and the other feels the helper's arm, then swap.
flow.context: This is the first step of Push-Pull Pairs. You guess before you feel.

flow.do: Your child bends the elbow slowly and then straightens it slowly. One hand stays on the front of the arm and one on the back. Ask them to tell you which muscle tightens at each stage.
flow.say: Bend your elbow slowly and then straighten it slowly. Keep your hands on the front and back of the arm. Which one tightens when? Do both ever work together?
flow.kid: Bend your elbow slowly. Then straighten it slowly. Feel both sides.

ask.q: What did you feel?
good: The front tightened when I bent.
The back tightened when I straightened.
I felt both when I went slowly.

flow.parent: The front muscle (biceps) bends the elbow, and the back muscle (triceps) straightens it. With nothing in your hand, you may feel the back muscle only faintly, because gravity does some of the straightening. That is why the next step pushes against a table.
flow.context: In this step, you feel the two muscles at the front and back of the arm.

flow.do: Your child sits at a table, elbow bent. One hand rests on the front and one on the back of the upper arm. Press the palm up under the table edge, then down on top. Feel which muscle tightens.
flow.say: Sit at the table. Keep one hand on the front and one on the back of your arm. Press your palm up under the table. Then press it down on top. Which muscle tightens each time?
flow.kid: Press up under the table. Then press down on top. Feel both muscles.
flow.parent: Pressing up under the table tightens the front muscle (biceps). Pressing down on top tightens the back muscle (triceps). Then hold a full water bottle and lower it slowly. The front muscle works hard even though the arm is going down, because it lets the weight down gradually. Ask your child to rate how tight each muscle feels, from 1 to 5. Press gently, never hard.

check.q: Why does the arm need both a muscle that bends and a muscle that straightens?
options: A muscle can only pull, so one is needed for each direction
One muscle is only for show
So the arm weighs more
check.why: A muscle can only pull. It cannot push. So the body uses a pair, one to pull the bone one way and one to pull it back. Smooth, steady movement comes from both working together.

flow.context: In this step, you feel both muscles working together to move the arm smoothly.

flow.do: Write a list of pairs together. Use the arm muscles, sweating and shivering, pupils opening and closing, and insulin and glucagon. Ask your child to add one pair of their own.
flow.say: Let us list the pairs we know. Arm muscles, sweating and shivering, pupils opening and closing, insulin and glucagon. Can you think of another pair that pulls or pushes in opposite directions?
flow.kid: List the pairs. Add one more of your own.
flow.parent: Other pairs: breathing in and out, heart speeding up and slowing, the two muscles that open and close the jaw, eating and feeling full. A strong answer says that a single control can push only one way, but a pair can correct in both directions and stop at the right place.
flow.think: Why might a pair be better than a single control?
flow.context: This is the last step of Push-Pull Pairs. You find the pattern in many parts of the body.

activities.title: Late Warmer-Colder: what delay does to a correction
activities.context: In this activity you play hide-and-seek with a coin, and find out why a correction that arrives late can swing past the target.

materials.item: a coin or a small stone (a spoon or a small toy also works)
a room with a clear floor, with chairs and toys moved away
a helper to call warmer and colder, and a second helper to count steps, if there are enough children

activities.record: Write the number of steps in Round 1, Round 2 and Round 3. Write one sentence on why the late calls made you swing.

setup.art: A child standing in a room with the helper hiding a coin behind a cushion, and a path of dotted footsteps.
setup.caption: 1. The helper hides a coin. You search by following warmer and colder.

setup.art: A child walking towards a coin with a speech bubble 'warmer' at once and a footstep count.
setup.caption: 2. Round 1. The calls come at once. Count your steps.

setup.art: A child walking past a coin with a speech bubble 'warmer' arriving late and the path swinging beyond the coin.
setup.caption: 3. Round 2. The calls come three seconds late. Keep walking and count your steps.

flow.do: Tell your child you will hide a coin in the room. They will search by following your calls of warmer and colder. Ask for a guess and a reason: what if you call a few seconds late?
flow.say: I will hide a coin. You will find it by following my calls of warmer and colder. First I call at once. Then I call three seconds late. Which way will be harder? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You search for a coin. I call warmer or colder. What if I call late?

ask.q: Why do you think late calls will make it harder?
good: I will already have moved.
The call will be about where I was.
I will walk past the coin.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. This works in any room, with just a coin or a small stone. For a fair test, hide the coin about the same distance from the start each round, in a spot the child has not seen. With two to four children, each takes a turn as the walker, the caller and the step counter. Use a different hiding place for each walker.
flow.context: This is the first step of Late Warmer-Colder. You guess before you play.

flow.do: Hide a coin about four metres from the start. Your child walks around the room, eyes open. Call 'warmer' if they get closer, and 'colder' if they move away. Call at once, each time. Count the steps they take until they find it.
flow.say: I will hide the coin while you wait outside. Walk around the room. I call warmer if you get closer. I call colder if you move away. I call as soon as you move. Count your steps.
flow.kid: Find the hidden coin. Count your steps. Your helper calls warmer or colder.
flow.parent: Hide the coin somewhere new for each round. Call as soon as the child moves. Count the steps they take.
flow.context: In this step, you play Warmer-Colder with calls that come at once. This is Round 1.

flow.do: Hide the coin in a new place at the same distance. Round 2: your child keeps walking at a steady pace. You count a slow three in your head before each call. Round 3: new place. They stop after each step and wait for the call.
flow.say: Round 2: keep walking, and I call three seconds late. Round 3: after each step, stop and wait for my call. Count your steps each time. Which round was the hardest?
flow.kid: Round 2: keep walking, calls come late. Round 3: stop and wait. Count your steps.

ask.q: What happened when the calls came late?
good: I walked past the coin.
I turned back too far.
I swung from side to side.

flow.parent: With late calls and a walker who keeps moving, children usually walk past the coin, then turn back too far. This is overshoot. In Round 3 the walker waits for each call. They find the coin without swinging, but with more steps and more time. This is the trade the body makes: gentle corrections, or predicting. If nobody overshoots in Round 2, make the delay longer or ask the walker to walk faster.

check.q: Why did the late calls make you walk past the coin?
options: The call told you about where you were before, not where you are now
The caller was tired
The coin moved
check.why: A delayed message is out of date. By the time it arrived, you had moved on. A correction based on old news overshoots. Small, slow steps give the message time to catch up.

flow.context: In this step, you play Warmer-Colder with calls that come late. This is Round 2.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what they thought, what they saw and why. Ask: where have you seen this swinging before?
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why did the late calls make you swing? Where have you seen swinging like this, like in a shower?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the calls were late, so the child moved past the target and swung. Other examples are a shower tap, a fridge that gets too cold and a driver steering in fog. Bodies cope by predicting and by making gentle corrections, as when your pancreas starts insulin when you smell food.
flow.think: What would a body need, to avoid swinging when its messages are slow?
flow.context: This is the last step of Late Warmer-Colder. You say what you found and why.

projects.title: My Daily Rhythm: a 3-day pulse diary
projects.context: In this three-day project you measure your resting pulse and breathing three times a day, and look for a daily pattern.

materials.item: a clock with seconds, or a phone timer (a stopwatch is not needed)
a notebook and a pencil
a helper to count breaths (a parent, brother or sister)

schedule.what: Make the table. Take your three readings today.
Take your three readings. Then look at all nine and find the pattern.

projects.record: Fill in the table with nine rows. Mark the highest and lowest pulse. Write one sentence about the pattern. If there is no clear pattern, say so. That is a real result.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of three rows (morning, afternoon, bedtime) and columns for pulse, breaths and mood.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with three rows and three columns.

setup.art: A child sitting quietly with two fingers on the wrist and a clock on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Sit for 3 minutes. Count your pulse for 15 seconds.

setup.art: A line drawn through nine pulse numbers with the highest and lowest marked.
setup.caption: 3. On Day 3, mark the highest and the lowest.

flow.do: Show your child how to find their pulse and count breaths. Ask for a guess and a reason: will the resting pulse be the same in the morning, afternoon and night?
flow.say: Today you will start a three-day diary. Three times a day you will measure your pulse and breathing at rest. Do you think the numbers will be the same at all times? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will measure your pulse three times a day. Will it be the same? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the numbers will be the same or different?
good: I am the same person all day.
I am sleepy in the morning.
I am busier in the afternoon.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Make the table together: three rows for morning, afternoon and bedtime, and columns for pulse in 15 seconds, breaths in 30 seconds and how I feel. With two to four children, each keeps their own table. They count each other's breaths and compare tables on Day 3.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Daily Rhythm. You guess before you start.

flow.do: Three times each day for three days, your child sits quietly for 3 minutes. Then they count the pulse for 15 seconds and a helper counts the breaths for 30 seconds. Write the numbers and one word for how they feel.
flow.say: Sit still for three minutes. Count your pulse for fifteen seconds. I will count your breaths for thirty seconds. Write the numbers, and one word for how you feel: sleepy, calm, excited, hungry.
flow.kid: Sit for three minutes. Count your pulse. Your helper counts your breaths.
flow.parent: Take the readings at about the same times each day: just after waking, mid-afternoon, and just before bed. Sit and rest first, because even walking to the chair raises the pulse. Excitement, worry, illness and a big meal can change the numbers. Write how your child felt, to see the pattern. Counting for 15 seconds is only accurate to a few beats, so a small difference between two readings may be noise.
flow.context: In this step, you take your measurements. You do this three times a day, for three days.

flow.do: On the last day, look at all nine rows. Mark the highest and the lowest pulse. Ask your child to say three things: what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Look at the table. Find the lowest pulse and the highest. When did they come? Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it changed?
flow.kid: Look at the table. Find the highest and lowest pulse. Say why.
flow.parent: Many children have a lower pulse in the early morning and a higher pulse later in the day, but excitement and hunger can change it, and the pattern may be small or unclear. Body warmth also follows a daily rhythm, typically lowest in the very early morning and highest in late afternoon. A strong answer says that the body's targets can move with the clock. This is allostasis. If your numbers show no pattern, say so and think why.
flow.think: Why might the body's set points change through the day?
flow.context: This is the last step of My Daily Rhythm. You look for a pattern in your numbers.

challenges.title: Steady-Level Tank: keep the level between two marks
challenges.problem: Build a bottle that keeps its water level between two tape marks, 4 centimetres apart, for two minutes. Start with the level between the marks. The tap trickle will be slow for the first test and about twice as fast for the second.
constraints: Use one clear bottle with its top cut off. You may use up to 3 holes, each made by a grown-up with a compass point.
The holes must all be about as wide as a ballpoint refill.
The tap trickle falls in at the top. You may not change the trickle.
The level must stay between the marks for two full minutes in each test. Fill the bottle to the lower mark before each test.
materials: a clear plastic bottle, about 1 litre, with the top cut off by a grown-up
a compass point or a fine nail, used by a grown-up
a ruler and tape, and a spare bottle in case a hole is too wide
a sink with a tap, a cup marked in millilitres and a clock or phone timer
general: One hole low down, as in the Level Bottle test. It works for one trickle speed.
A bigger hole, so more water leaves when the trickle is fast. But then the slow trickle may never fill the bottle to the lower mark.
A tall bottle with holes at two heights.
creative: A second hole placed near the top mark, so it joins in only when the level is high. It works like a second control that wakes up when the first is not enough.
A short pipe or straw at the top mark that acts as an overflow, like the overflow pipe in a roof tank.
Three holes at three heights, so the push back grows step by step as the level climbs.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Build it, test it with the slow trickle and the fast one, and change one thing. Which design held the level between the marks? Why do you think it worked?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about steady levels. You build a bottle that keeps its level when the trickle changes.

setup.art: A child sketching three bottle designs on paper, one with a single hole, one with two holes at different heights and one with a straw overflow.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some designs on paper.

setup.art: A bottle with two tape marks and a ruler, holes at different heights, standing in a sink.
setup.caption: 2. Build the bottle. Mark the two levels.

setup.art: A tap trickle entering the bottle with the water level between the marks and a clock showing two minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Test with a slow trickle and a fast trickle.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to sketch two or three bottle designs on paper, with the holes drawn at different heights.
flow.say: Your bottle must keep its water level between two tape marks, even when the tap trickle changes. Draw some ideas first. Where will the holes go? How many?
flow.kid: Draw some bottle designs. Where will the holes go?

ask.q: What would make a bottle keep its level when the trickle gets faster?
good: A bigger hole.
A second hole higher up.
A hole that opens only when the level is high.

flow.parent: Do not give the answer. Many children try a bigger hole first. Let them test it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the challenge. You plan before you build.

flow.do: A grown-up makes the holes with a compass point. Tape two marks on the bottle, one at 5 centimetres and one at 9 centimetres above the base. Tape a ruler beside them.
flow.say: A grown-up makes the holes with the sharp point. Put tape marks at five and nine centimetres. Your level must stay between those marks for two minutes.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes the holes. Tape two marks on the bottle.
flow.parent: Holes are made with a compass point by a grown-up, and the cut edge is taped. Each is about as wide as a ballpoint refill. A hole near the base lets out water fast when the level is high. A second hole at the 7 centimetre mark joins in only when the level rises that high. The right hole heights depend on your tap, so expect to try several designs. With two to four children, each pair builds a design, and the pairs compare.
flow.context: In this step, you build the Steady-Level Tank.

flow.do: Fill the bottle to the lower mark. Run the tap at about 20 millilitres in 10 seconds. Does the level stay between the marks for 2 minutes? Then try about 40 millilitres in 10 seconds.
flow.say: Fill the bottle to the lower mark. Run the slow trickle for two minutes. Is the level between the marks? Now try the faster trickle. Is it still between the marks?
flow.kid: Test a slow trickle. Then a fast trickle. Does the level stay between the marks?

ask.q: What happened to the level when the trickle got faster?
good: It rose.
It stayed between the marks.
It went over the top mark.

flow.parent: A single hole will usually rise past the top mark when the trickle doubles. A second hole higher up joins in when the level climbs, and holds it back. Your exact numbers depend on the hole sizes and the tap, so write down what you see. If no design holds, say which one came closest. This is like a body adding another control when the first is not enough.
flow.context: In this step, you test your tank with two different trickle speeds.

flow.do: Change one thing, such as the height of the second hole. Test the fast trickle again. Write down which design held the level best.
flow.say: Change one thing only. Move the second hole, or make it a little bigger. Test the fast trickle again. Which design holds the level best?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Which design is best?
flow.parent: Changing only one thing lets your child see which change helped. Write down each version and what happened.

check.q: Why change only one thing at a time?
options: So you know which change made the difference
Because changing two things is not allowed
To save water
check.why: If you change two things and the result improves, you cannot tell which change helped. One change at a time makes it a fair test.

quiz.p: What makes a level stay steady?
opts: What flows in matches what flows out
Nothing moving at all
A single push in one direction
quiz.why: A level is steady when the flow in equals the flow out. If one flow wins, the level rises or falls.

quiz.p: You pour a cup of water into a Level Bottle that was steady. The level jumps up. What happens next?
opts: The level falls back to where it was
The level stays high
The level rises until the bottle overflows
quiz.why: Deeper water leaks faster, so the leak is bigger than the trickle until the level has come back down. The change causes its own push back.

quiz.p: Which pair is correct for the sugar in the blood?
opts: Insulin lowers it and glucagon raises it
Insulin raises it and glucagon lowers it
Both of them raise it
quiz.why: Insulin tells cells to take sugar in, which lowers the level. Glucagon tells the liver to release sugar, which raises it.

quiz.p: Where in the body are insulin and glucagon made?
opts: In the pancreas
In the liver
In the heart
quiz.why: Beta cells in the pancreas make insulin and alpha cells make glucagon. The liver is where sugar is stored and released.

quiz.p: What is the main signal that makes you want to breathe?
opts: Carbon dioxide building up in the blood
Oxygen disappearing from the air
A tired feeling in the lungs
quiz.why: Sensors in the brainstem notice carbon dioxide in the blood and speed up breathing. Low oxygen matters mainly at very high altitude.

quiz.p: Just after you stop running, your pulse is high. What does it do in the next minutes?
opts: It falls fast at first and then more slowly
It falls at the same speed all the way
It stays high for an hour
quiz.why: The further the pulse is from rest, the faster it falls. That is why the biggest drop comes in the first minute.

quiz.p: A bright light comes on and your pupils shrink at once. What decided this?
opts: An automatic loop through the brainstem
Your decision to protect your eyes
The light itself changed your eyes
quiz.why: Light on the eye sends a signal to the brainstem, which tightens the ring muscles. It happens in under a second, before you could decide anything.

quiz.p: Why does a shower swing between too hot and too cold when the water is slow to arrive?
opts: The correction arrives late, so you overshoot
Hot water and cold water do not mix
The tap gets tired
quiz.why: A correction based on old news goes past the target. Waiting between small turns of the tap stops the swinging.

quiz.p: What is missing in a person with type 1 diabetes?
opts: Insulin, because the cells that make it have been destroyed
Glucagon
Sugar in the food
quiz.why: The body's own defences destroy the beta cells, so almost no insulin is made. People take insulin from outside.

quiz.p: A steady level is a place where nothing is happening.
quiz.why: False. A steady level is made of flows that match. In the bottle, in the ankle and in the blood, something is always moving.

quiz.p: Why does an arm have one muscle that bends the elbow and another that straightens it?
opts: A muscle can only pull, so each direction needs its own muscle
One muscle is a spare
Two muscles make the arm look bigger
quiz.why: A muscle can pull but not push. So the body uses a pair, one to pull one way and one to pull back.

quiz.p: Which statement about diabetes is correct?
opts: There are different kinds, and eating sweets is not the cause of all of them
Everyone who has it ate too many sweets
Nothing can be done for it today
quiz.why: Type 1 is caused by the body's defences destroying insulin-making cells. Type 2 has many causes. Both can be managed with good medical care.

open_questions.q: Why does the immune system destroy the insulin-making cells in type 1 diabetes?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that genes and something in the environment are involved, but they do not know exactly what starts it.

open_questions.q: Why do the body's cells respond less well to insulin in type 2 diabetes?
open_questions.why_open: Many causes have been found, including body fat and inactivity, but how they fit together is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Can the cells that make insulin be replaced?
open_questions.why_open: Early trials of new insulin-making cells are under way. The results so far are small, and long-term safety is still being checked.

open_questions.q: Does the body have a set point, or does it predict and move its targets all the time?
open_questions.why_open: Both views explain many results. Scientists do not agree on which picture is better for each loop.

open_questions.q: Why does the urge to breathe feel like something, and not just happen?
open_questions.why_open: How the brain makes feelings at all is not known. It is part of the biggest open question in science.

maths.problem: A small cola bottle has 26 grams of sugar. A level teaspoon holds 4 grams. About how many teaspoons are in the bottle, and about how many times more is that than the 1 teaspoon in all of a grown-up's blood?
maths.answer: About 6 teaspoons, and about 6 times more.
maths.explain: 26 divided by 4 is 6, with 2 left over, so about 6 teaspoons. One teaspoon in the blood goes into 6 teaspoons six times.
maths.context: In One Teaspoon, you turn grams of sugar on a label into teaspoons you can see.
maths.why_maths: Dividing grams by a teaspoon's weight turns a number on a label into something you can picture, so you can compare it with the sugar in your blood.

maths.problem: In the Level Bottle, the trickle fills 30 millilitres in 10 seconds. How many millilitres would the trickle give in one minute? If the hole lets out 20 millilitres every 10 seconds, how many millilitres stay in the bottle in one minute?
maths.answer: 180 millilitres in a minute. 60 millilitres stay in.
maths.explain: A minute has six lots of 10 seconds. 30 times 6 is 180. The hole lets out 20 times 6, which is 120. 180 take away 120 is 60 millilitres that stay in the bottle.
maths.context: In the Level Bottle test, you catch the trickle in a cup for 10 seconds and watch the level.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the water in and the water out tells you whether the level will rise, fall or stay put.

maths.problem: Aarav's pulse is 80 beats a minute at rest. After exercise it is 140. Two minutes after stopping it is 100. Did his pulse fall by more than half of the rise by then? How do you know?
maths.answer: No. It fell by 40, and the rise was 60, so it fell by two thirds of the rise. That is more than half.
maths.explain: The rise was 140 take away 80, which is 60. The fall was 140 take away 100, which is 40. 40 out of 60 is two thirds, which is more than half. So yes, it fell by more than half.
maths.context: In the Recovery Race, you count your pulse every minute after exercise and watch it come back.
maths.why_maths: Comparing how much of the rise has gone lets you say how quickly different people or efforts recover, even when their starting pulses differ.

maths.problem: A bottle gets 6 millilitres of water every second and loses 4 millilitres every second through the hole. After 10 seconds, how much more water is in the bottle? What must happen to the leak for the level to become steady?
maths.answer: 20 millilitres more. The leak must grow to 6 millilitres a second.
maths.explain: 6 take away 4 is 2 more each second, and 2 times 10 is 20 millilitres. The level is steady only when the water out equals the water in, so the leak must become 6 a second.
maths.context: In the Level Bottle test, the level rises until the leak matches the trickle.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the flow out from the flow in shows whether a level will rise, fall or stay steady.

maths.problem: Tara breathes 20 times a minute at rest. How many breaths is that in one day? Is it more or less than 30,000?
maths.explain: 20 times 60 is 1,200 in an hour. 1,200 times 24 is 28,800 in a day. 28,800 is less than 30,000.
maths.context: In the Recovery Race, you count your breaths, and find your resting number.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a small steady rate by a long time shows how much work a steady loop does without a break.

roots.context: We have kept a bottle's level, a pulse, a pupil and a blood sugar steady. Now we ask what this kind of steadiness tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A steady level is not a place where nothing happens. It is two opposite pushes that keep meeting. Insulin pulls sugar out of your blood while glucagon puts it back. Where they balance, the level stays flat.
deep_truth.habit: We treat 'steady' and 'still' as if they meant the same thing, so a flat line looks like nothing is going on. But a flat line can hide a great deal of work.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Level Bottle, the level stopped rising while water poured in and out the whole time. On one leg, the ankle looked still only because it kept pulling both ways. If your own results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: You are a shape that is held, not a thing that sits. Your ankle, your sugar and your pupils are corrected hundreds of times a minute so that you can look the same.
three.what_is_life: A living body stays itself by keeping things flowing through it: food and water in, heat and waste out. The level stays while the stuff changes.
three.what_is_this_world: A river keeps its shape while its water changes every second. A star keeps its size because gravity pulling in meets pressure pushing out.

roots.thread: From one source come pairs: in and out, up and down, pull and push. Each pair adds up to a balance. In the bottle, the trickle and the leak meet at one level. In the ankle, left meets right. In the blood, insulin meets glucagon. In a star, gravity meets pressure. The steady things we see are places where two pushes meet, and nothing at the centre has to hold them still.

teachings.teaching: As paraphrased, the Way of heaven is like the bending of a bow. The high is brought down and the low is raised up. What has too much is reduced and what has too little is given more.
teachings.link: This is a loop that pushes back. Where there is too much, it takes away. Where there is too little, it adds. Insulin and glucagon do exactly this with sugar.

teachings.teaching: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker of about 500 BCE, said that on those who step into the same rivers, different and different waters flow.
teachings.link: A river looks the same while its water is always new. The level in the bottle and the sugar in your blood are the same, steady while their stuff keeps changing.

teachings.teaching: As paraphrased, Krishna says that a steady practice is not for one who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little. It belongs to one who is moderate in eating, play, sleep and waking.
teachings.link: The Gita is speaking about the mind and the way we live. But it names the same thing as the body does: balance comes from neither too much nor too little, kept up all the time.

science.text: Claude Bernard, a French physiologist, argued in the 1800s that a steady inner world is the condition for a free life. Walter Cannon named the idea homeostasis in 1926.
A star stays steady for billions of years because gravity pulling inwards balances pressure pushing outwards.
Some scientists think the body's set points are targets that it moves to suit the day, rather than fixed numbers. This view is called allostasis.

other_view.view: A bottle with a hole, a blood sugar loop and a star are all fully explained by physics and chemistry. Calling them meetings of opposite pushes is a way of describing them, and nothing more is needed. Looking for a deeper pattern is something people add.

practice.title: Feel the sway
practice.say: Stand with your feet apart and your eyes soft. Stay as still as you can. Notice your body swaying a tiny bit, forwards and back, left and right. Feel your ankles and feet making small corrections. Breathe in and out slowly three times. Notice that your breath is also two pushes, in and out. Stay with that for a moment.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Level Bottle: the bottle, hole and tap trickle were worked out from the way water leaves a hole, so the steady level rises as the trickle speeds up. The exact levels depend on the hole and the tap, so the steps say to write down what you see. A hole that is too big never fills, and a trickle that is too fast goes over the rim, and the steps say what to do then. Recovery Race: a grown-up must stay with the child. Pulse counting is hard at first, so practise at rest. Pupil Gauge: very dark brown eyes make the pupil hard to see, so a lamp at the side or a phone film is suggested. Sugar See-Saw: the cards and the rules were read through for a full game, but not played with a real family. Late Warmer-Colder works in any room. Facts checked against sources: about 4 to 5 grams of glucose in a grown-up's blood (Harvard BioNumbers gives about 4 g, so 'about' stays), the resting pulse and breathing ranges (softened to 16 to 25 breaths), about 101 million people with diabetes in India (Lancet 2023), ants and honey urine in the Sushruta texts (secondary sources only), and the one-dollar patent sale (confirmed; 'each' removed). The flies story is disputed and was removed. The three videos have no address yet.
